Bifurcations and Spectral Stability of Solitary Waves in Coupled Nonlinear Schrödinger EquationsThanks: This work was partially supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number JP17H02859.

Kazuyuki Yagasaki and Shotaro Yamazoe Address: Department of Applied Mathematics and Physics, Graduate School of Informatics, Kyoto University, Yoshida-Honmachi, Sakyo-ku, Kyoto 606-8501, JAPAN Email address: yagasaki@amp.i.kyoto-u.ac.jp (K. Yagasaki) Email address: yamazoe@amp.i.kyoto-u.ac.jp (S. Yamazoe)
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We study bifurcations and spectral stability of solitary waves in coupled nonlinear Schrödinger (CNLS) equations on the line. We assume that the coupled equations possess a solution of which one component is identically zero, and call it a fundamental solitary wave. By using a result of one of the authors and his collaborator, pitchfork bifurcations of the fundamental solitary wave are detected. We utilize the Hamiltonian-Krein index theory and Evans function technique to determine the spectral or orbital stability of the bifurcated solitary waves as well as that of the fundamental one under some nondegenerate conditions which are easy to verify, compared with those of the previous results. We apply our theory to CNLS equations with a cubic nonlinearity and give numerical evidences for the theoretical results.

Key words and phrases: 
bifurcation, coupled nonlinear Schrödinger equations, solitary wave, spectral stability
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
35B32, 35B35, 35Q55, 37K45, 37K50

1. Introduction

We consider coupled nonlinear Schrödinger (CNLS) equations of the form

i​∂tu+∂x2u+∂1F⁡(|u|2,|v|2,μ)​u=0,i​∂tv+∂x2v+∂2F⁡(|u|2,|v|2,μ)​v=0,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{i}\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}^{2}u+\partial_{1}F(|u|^{2},|v|^{2};\mu)u=0,\\ &\mathrm{i}\partial_{t}v+\partial_{x}^{2}v+\partial_{2}F(|u|^{2},|v|^{2};\mu)v=0,\end{aligned} (1.1)

where (u,v)=(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))(u,v)=(u(t,x),v(t,x)) are complex-valued unknown functions of (t,x)∈ℝ×ℝ(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}, μ\mu is a real parameter, F:ℝ×ℝ×ℝ→ℝF:\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is a given function, and ∂jF\partial_{j}F represents the derivative of FF with respect to the jj-th argument for j=1,2j=1,2. Our special attention is paid to the cubic nonlinearity,

F⁡(ζ1,ζ2,β1)=12​ζ12+β1​ζ1​ζ2+β22​ζ22,\displaystyle F(\zeta_{1},\zeta_{2};\beta_{1})=\frac{1}{2}\zeta_{1}^{2}+\beta_{1}\zeta_{1}\zeta_{2}+\frac{\beta_{2}}{2}\zeta_{2}^{2}, (1.2)

where β1,β2\beta_{1},\beta_{2} are real constants and β1\beta_{1} is taken as the control parameter μ\mu below. In applications, (1.1) arises when considering propagation of two interacted waves in nonlinear media. For example, in nonlinear optics, it describes nonlinear pulse propagation in birefringent fibers. See [2, 27, 34, 39] and references therein. (1.1) has a Hamiltonian structure with the Hamiltonian

ℋ⁡(u,v,μ)=12​∫ℝ(|∂xu⁡(x)|2+|∂xv⁡(x)|2−F⁡(|u|2,|v|2,μ))​𝑑x,\displaystyle\mathcal{H}(u,v;\mu)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\Bigl(|\partial_{x}u(x)|^{2}+|\partial_{x}v(x)|^{2}-F(|u|^{2},|v|^{2};\mu)\Bigr)\mathrm{d}x,

and the Cauchy problem of (1.1) is well-posed in the Sobolev space H1​(ℝ,ℂ2)H^{1}(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}^{2}) (see, e.g., Section 4 of [7]).

Here we are interested in solitary waves of the form

u⁡(t,x)=ei⁡(ω​t+c​x−c2​t+θ)​U​(x−2​c​t−x0),v⁡(t,x)=ei⁡(s​t+c​x−c2​t+ϕ)​V​(x−2​c​t−x0),\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &u(t,x)=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\omega t+cx-c^{2}t+\theta)}U(x-2ct-x_{0}),\\ &v(t,x)=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(st+cx-c^{2}t+\phi)}V(x-2ct-x_{0}),\end{aligned} (1.3)

such that the real-valued functions (U,V)=(U⁡(x),V⁡(x))(U,V)=(U(x),V(x)) satisfy U⁡(x),V⁡(x)→0U(x),V(x)\to 0 as x→±∞x\to\pm\infty, where cc, x0x_{0}, θ\theta, ϕ\phi, and ω,s>0\omega,s>0 are real constants. Henceforth, without loss of generality, we take c,x0,θ,ϕ=0c,x_{0},\theta,\phi=0 by scaling the independent variables if necessary, since (1.1) is invariant under the Galilean transformations

(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))↦ei⁡(c​x−c2​t)​(u⁡(t,x−2​c​t),v⁡(t,x−2​c​t)),c∈ℝ,\displaystyle(u(t,x),v(t,x))\mapsto\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(cx-c^{2}t)}(u(t,x-2ct),v(t,x-2ct)),\quad c\in\mathbb{R},

the spatial translations

(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))↦(u⁡(t,x−x0),v⁡(t,x−x0)),x0∈ℝ,\displaystyle(u(t,x),v(t,x))\mapsto(u(t,x-x_{0}),v(t,x-x_{0})),\quad x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}, (1.4)

and the gauge transformations

(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))↦(ei​θ​u​(t,x),ei​ϕ​v​(t,x)),θ,ϕ∈ℝ.\displaystyle(u(t,x),v(t,x))\mapsto(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}u(t,x),\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\phi}v(t,x)),\quad\theta,\phi\in\mathbb{R}. (1.5)

So (U,V)=(U⁡(x),V⁡(x))(U,V)=(U(x),V(x)) solves

−U′′+ω​U−∂1F⁡(U2,V2,μ)​U=0,−V′′+s​V−∂2F⁡(U2,V2,μ)​V=0,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &-U^{\prime\prime}+\omega U-\partial_{1}F(U^{2},V^{2};\mu)U=0,\\ &-V^{\prime\prime}+sV-\partial_{2}F(U^{2},V^{2};\mu)V=0,\end{aligned} (1.6)

where the prime represents the differentiation with respect to xx. Throughout this paper we assume that (1.6) possess a homoclinic solution of the form (U,V)=(U0​(x),0)(U,V)=(U_{0}(x),0). This assumption holds with U0​(x)=2​ω​sech⁡(ω​x)U_{0}(x)=\sqrt{2\omega}\sech(\sqrt{\omega}x) for the particular nonlinearity (1.2). We refer to the solitary wave of the form

(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))=(ei​ω​t​U0​(x),0),\displaystyle(u(t,x),v(t,x))=(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}U_{0}(x),0), (1.7)

as a fundamental solitary wave. Obviously, (U,V)=(−U0​(x),0)(U,V)=(-U_{0}(x),0) is also a homoclinic solution to (1.6) but it gives the same solitary wave (1.3) as (1.7) if θ=π\theta=\pi is taken. So we only treat (1.7).

Blázquez-Sanz and Yagasaki [6] studied bifurcations of homoclinic orbits in a large class of ordinary differential equations using Gruendler’s version of Melnikov’s method [17], and applied their theory to show that infinitely many pitchfork bifurcations of (U,V)=(U0​(x),0)(U,V)=(U_{0}(x),0) occur in (1.6) with (1.2) when β1\beta_{1} is taken as a control parameter. Moreover, in a general situation, they proved that if bifurcations of homoclinic orbits occur, then the associated variational equations, i.e., linearized equations, around the homoclinic orbits are integrable in the meaning of differential Galois theory [32]. Homoclinic orbits born at the pitchfork bifurcations in (1.6) correspond to solitary waves of the form (1.3) with nonzero UU- and VV-components, which are often called vector solitons, bifurcated from the fundamental solitary waves (1.7) in (1.1).

Once establishing their existence, the stability problem of these bifurcated solitary waves naturally arises. Ohta [28] proved the orbital stability of the fundamental solitary waves in (1.1) with (1.2) and β2=1\beta_{2}=1. Subsequently, his result was extended to more general nonlinearity cases by several authors [5, 8, 25, 26, 27]. All of these results are based on variational characterizations of solitary waves. On the other hand, the spectral stability of vector solitons in (1.1) with (1.2) or the saturable nonlinearity was discussed by Pelinovsky and Yang [31]. They employed the Hamiltonian-Krein index theory, which was established by Pelinovsky [30] and Kapitula et al. [18, 19] independently, and carried out some formal calculations to claim that any purely imaginary embedded eigenvalue with a positive (resp. negative) Krein signature disappears (resp. changes to a pair of eigenvalues with nonzero real parts) after bifurcations. This suggests that the bifurcated solitary waves of (1.1) with (1.2) are spectrally stable and unstable, respectively, when they have positive and sign-changing VV-components. A rigorous analysis was given by Cuccagna et al. [10] using a technique based on the analytic continuation of the resolvent. Moreover, some nondegenerate conditions which are generically satisfied but difficult to verify for concrete examples were assumed there. Li and Promislow [24] also studied the spectral stability of solitary waves in CNLS equations with a different special nonlinearity, using the Evans function technique. This technique was first proposed in Evans’ earlier works about the stability of pulse solutions in nerve axon equations [12, 13, 14, 15], and subsequently discussed in a topological framework by Alexander et al. [3].

In this paper, we study pitchfork bifurcations of the fundamental solitary waves detected by the Melnikov analysis of [6] in (1.1) and determine the spectral and/or orbital stability of the fundamental and bifurcated solitary waves under some nondegenerate conditions which are easy to verify, compared with those of [10, 31]. Here the terminology “pitchfork bifurcation” is used with caution: a pair of homoclinic solutions to (1.6), which correspond to the same family of solitary waves of the form (1.3) in (1.1), are born at the bifurcation point. Our main tool to determine their spectral stability is the Evans function technique as in [24] but more careful treatments are required. The Hamiltonian-Krein index theory is also used as in [31]. We apply our theory to the particular nonlinearity case of (1.2): pitchfork bifurcations of the fundamental solitary waves are detected and the spectral or orbital stability of the fundamental and bifurcated solitary waves are determined for almost all parameter values. In particular, the nondegenerate conditions for bifurcations and spectral stability are given explicitly. The theoretical results are also demonstrated with numerical computations obtained by the computer tool AUTO [11].

The outline of this paper is as follows: In Section 2, we state our assumptions and main results on pitchfork bifurcations of the fundamental solitary waves in (1.1). In Section 3, we use the Melnikov analysis of [6] for (1.6) and prove the main result on pitchfork bifurcations. For the reader’s convenience, in our setting, the Melnikov analysis is briefly reviewed. In Section 4, we present the Hamiltonian-Krein index theory and Evans function technique in appropriate forms. Applying these approaches, we prove the main results on the stability of the fundamental and bifurcated solitary waves in Sections 5 and 6, respectively. Finally, we illustrate our theory for the particular nonlinearity (1.2) along with some numerical computations in Section 7.

2. Main Results

In this section, we give our assumptions and main results on bifurcations of the fundamental solitary wave (1.7) and the stability of the fundamental and bifurcated solitary waves in the CNLS equations (1.1).

2.1. Bifurcations of the Fundamental Solitary Wave

We first make the following assumptions.

  • (A1)

    F:ℝ×ℝ×ℝ→ℝF:\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is a C3C^{3} function satisfying

    F⁡(0,0,μ)=∂1F⁡(0,0,μ)=∂2F⁡(0,0,μ)=0,∂μF⁡(ζ,0,μ)=0,\displaystyle F(0,0;\mu)=\partial_{1}F(0,0;\mu)=\partial_{2}F(0,0;\mu)=0,\quad\partial_{\mu}F(\zeta,0;\mu)=0,

  • (A2)

    When V=0V=0, the first equation of (1.6),

    −U′′+ω​U−∂1F⁡(U2,0)​U=0,\displaystyle-U^{\prime\prime}+\omega U-\partial_{1}F(U^{2},0)U=0,

    has a homoclinic solution U0​(x)≢0U_{0}(x)\not\equiv 0 such that limx→±∞U0​(x)=0\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}U_{0}(x)=0 and U0′​(0)=0U_{0}^{\prime}(0)=0.

  • (A3)

    For some μ0∈ℝ\mu_{0}\in\mathbb{R}, the normal variational equation of (1.6) around the homoclinic orbit (U,V)=(U0​(x),0)(U,V)=(U_{0}(x),0),

    −δ​V′′+s​δ​V−∂2F⁡(U0​(x)2,0,μ0)​δ​V=0,\displaystyle-\delta V^{\prime\prime}+s\delta V-\partial_{2}F(U_{0}(x)^{2},0;\mu_{0})\delta V=0, (2.1)

    has a nonzero bounded solution δ​V=V1​(x)\delta V=V_{1}(x) such that limx→±∞V1​(x)=0\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}V_{1}(x)=0. Henceforth we take μ0=0\mu_{0}=0 by shifting the value of μ\mu if necessary without loss of generality.

Applying the Melnikov analysis of [6] reviewed in Section 3.1, we have the following bifurcation result.

Theorem 2.2.

Suppose that (A1)-(A3) and a¯2,b¯2≠0\bar{a}_{2},\bar{b}_{2}\neq 0 hold. Then a pitchfork bifurcation of the fundamental solitary wave (1.7) occurs at μ=0\mu=0. In addition, it is supercritical or subcritical, depending on whether a¯2​b¯2<0\bar{a}_{2}\bar{b}_{2}<0 or >0>0. Moreover, the bifurcated solitary waves are written as

(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))=(ei​ω​t​Uε​(x),ei​s​t​Vε​(x))\displaystyle(u(t,x),v(t,x))=(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}U_{\varepsilon}(x),\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}st}V_{\varepsilon}(x)) (2.5)

Uε​(x)=U0​(x)+ε2​U2​(x)+O⁡(ε4),Vε​(x)=±(ε​V1​(x)+O⁡(ε3)),\displaystyle U_{\varepsilon}(x)=U_{0}(x)+\varepsilon^{2}U_{2}(x)+O(\varepsilon^{4}),\quad V_{\varepsilon}(x)=\pm(\varepsilon V_{1}(x)+O(\varepsilon^{3})), (2.6)

where ε>0\varepsilon>0 is a small parameter such that

μ=μ¯ε2,μ¯⋅⋅=−b¯2/a¯2.\displaystyle\mu=\bar{\mu}\,\varepsilon^{2},\qquad\bar{\mu}\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}\hss}\raisebox{-1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}}=-{\bar{b}_{2}}/{\bar{a}_{2}}. (2.7)

A proof of Theorem 2.2 is given in Section 3.

2.2. Stability of the Fundamental and Bifurcated Solitary Waves

We turn to the stability of the fundamental and bifurcated solitary waves. We begin with the definition of orbital stability.

Definition 2.3.

The solitary wave (2.8) is orbitally stable if for any ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exists a constant δ>0\delta>0 such that for all (u0,v0)∈H1​(ℝ,ℂ2)(u_{0},v_{0})\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}^{2}) with

infx0,θ,ϕ∈ℝ(∥u0−ei​θU(⋅−x0)∥H1+∥v0−ei​ϕV(⋅−x0)∥H1)<δ,\displaystyle\inf_{x_{0},\theta,\phi\in\mathbb{R}}\bigl(\|u_{0}-\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}U(\cdot-x_{0})\|_{H^{1}}+\|v_{0}-\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\phi}V(\cdot-x_{0})\|_{H^{1}}\bigr)<\delta,

the solution (u⁡(t),v⁡(t))∈C⁡(ℝ,H1​(ℝ,ℂ2))(u(t),v(t))\in C(\mathbb{R},H^{1}(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}^{2})) to (1.1) with (u⁡(0),v⁡(0))=(u0,v0)(u(0),v(0))=(u_{0},v_{0}) satisfies

supt∈ℝinfx0,θ,ϕ∈ℝ(∥u(t)−ei​θU(⋅−x0)∥H1+∥v(t)−ei​ϕV(⋅−x0)∥H1)<ε.\displaystyle\sup_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\inf_{x_{0},\theta,\phi\in\mathbb{R}}\bigl(\|u(t)-\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}U(\cdot-x_{0})\|_{H^{1}}+\|v(t)-\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\phi}V(\cdot-x_{0})\|_{H^{1}}\bigr)<\varepsilon.

Otherwise, it is orbitally unstable.

The linearized operator ℒ:H2​(ℝ,ℂ4)\mathscr{L}:H^{2}(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}^{4}) ⊂L2​(ℝ,ℂ4)→L2​(ℝ,ℂ4)\subset L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}^{4})\to L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}^{4}) around the solitary wave

(u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x))=(ei​ω​t​U​(x),ei​s​t​V​(x))\displaystyle(u(t,x),v(t,x))=(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}U(x),\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}st}V(x)) (2.8)

is given by

ℒ=−iΣ3[−∂x2I4+(ω​I2O2O2s​I2)−(B11​(x)B12​(x)B21​(x)B22​(x))]\displaystyle\mathscr{L}=-\mathrm{i}\Sigma_{3}\left[-\partial_{x}^{2}I_{4}+\begin{pmatrix}\omega I_{2}&O_{2}\\ O_{2}&sI_{2}\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}B_{11}(x)&B_{12}(x)\\ B_{21}(x)&B_{22}(x)\end{pmatrix}\right] (2.9)

where InI_{n} and OnO_{n}, respectively, represents the n×nn\times n identity and zero matrices, and

σ1=(0110),σ3=(100−1),Σ3=(σ3O2O2σ3),\displaystyle\sigma_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\sigma_{3}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad\Sigma_{3}=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{3}&O_{2}\\ O_{2}&\sigma_{3}\end{pmatrix},
B11​(x)=∂12F⁡(U​(x)2,V​(x)2)​U​(x)2​(I2+σ1)+∂1F⁡(U​(x)2,V​(x)2)​I2,\displaystyle B_{11}(x)=\partial_{1}^{2}F(U(x)^{2},V(x)^{2})U(x)^{2}(I_{2}+\sigma_{1})+\partial_{1}F(U(x)^{2},V(x)^{2})I_{2},
B12​(x)=B21​(x)=∂1∂2F⁡(U​(x)2,V​(x)2)​U​(x)​V​(x)​(I2+σ1),\displaystyle B_{12}(x)=B_{21}(x)=\partial_{1}\partial_{2}F(U(x)^{2},V(x)^{2})U(x)V(x)(I_{2}+\sigma_{1}),
B22​(x)=∂22F⁡(U​(x)2,V​(x)2)​V​(x)2​(I2+σ1)+∂2F⁡(U​(x)2,V​(x)2)​I2.\displaystyle B_{22}(x)=\partial_{2}^{2}F(U(x)^{2},V(x)^{2})V(x)^{2}(I_{2}+\sigma_{1})+\partial_{2}F(U(x)^{2},V(x)^{2})I_{2}.

See Section 4.1 for the derivation of ℒ\mathscr{L}. We easily show that the essential spectrum of ℒ\mathscr{L} is given by

σess(ℒ)=i(−∞,−min{ω,s}]∪i[min{ω,s},∞).\displaystyle\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathscr{L})=\mathrm{i}(-\infty,-\min\{\omega,s\}]\cup\mathrm{i}[\min\{\omega,s\},\infty).

Moreover, σ⁡(ℒ)\sigma(\mathscr{L}) is symmetric with respect to the real and imaginary axis: if λ∈σ⁡(ℒ)\lambda\in\sigma(\mathscr{L}), then −λ,±λ∗∈σ⁡(ℒ)-\lambda,\pm\lambda^{*}\in\sigma(\mathscr{L}), where the superscript ‘∗\ast’ represents the complex conjugate.

Definition 2.4.

The solitary wave (2.8) in (1.1) is spectrally stable if the spectrum σ⁡(ℒ)\sigma(\mathscr{L}) of ℒ\mathscr{L} is contained in the closed left half plane. Otherwise, it is spectrally unstable.

For the fundamental and bifurcated solitary waves, we have the following theorems.

Theorem 2.5.

For any μ∈ℝ\mu\in\mathbb{R}, the fundamental solitary wave (1.7) is orbitally and spectrally stable if ∂ω‖U0‖L22>0\partial_{\omega}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}>0, and it is orbitally and spectrally unstable if ∂ω‖U0‖L22<0\partial_{\omega}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}<0.

Theorem 2.6.

Let ℓ\ell be the number of zeros of V1​(x)V_{1}(x). For ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small, the bifurcated solitary waves (2.5) are orbitally and spectrally stable if ∂ω‖U0‖L22>0\partial_{\omega}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}>0 and ℓ=0\ell=0, and it is orbitally and spectrally unstable if ∂ω‖U0‖L22<0\partial_{\omega}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}<0.

Proofs of Theorem 2.5 and 2.6 are given in Sections 5 and 6.1, respectively. Note that Theorem 2.6 says nothing about the stability of the bifurcated solitary waves with ℓ>0\ell>0 when ∂ω‖U0‖L22>0\partial_{\omega}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}>0. We assume that ∂ω‖U0‖L22>0\partial_{\omega}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}>0 and discuss the stability of bifurcated solitary waves in the rest of this section.

Let ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0} and ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon}, respectively, denote the linearized operator around the fundamental and bifurcated solitary waves. To determine the spectral stability of the bifurcated solitary waves, we need to discuss how purely imaginary eigenvalues of ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0} change when ε>0\varepsilon>0. Let E⁡(λ,ε)E(\lambda,\varepsilon) denote the Evans function for ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon}, which allows us to describe the changes of these eigenvalues for ε>0\varepsilon>0. See Section 4.3 for its definition. Especially, a zero of E⁡(λ,ε)E(\lambda,\varepsilon) is typically an eigenvalue of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} but is not necessarily so, and it is called a resonance pole if not (e.g., Chapter 9 of [20]). We also see that the Evans function E⁡(λ,ε)E(\lambda,\varepsilon) may not be analytic at λ∈{±i​ω,±i​s}\lambda\in\{\pm\mathrm{i}\omega,\pm\mathrm{i}s\}, which is a branch point for a square root function in (2.14) or (2.17) below (see also Section 4.3) and at which the corresponding Jost solutions may lose their analyticity in λ\lambda. Near λ=λbr\lambda=\lambda_{\mathrm{br}} with λbr∈{±i​ω,±i​s}\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}\in\{\pm\mathrm{i}\omega,\pm\mathrm{i}s\}, using the transformation γ2=±i⁡(λ−λbr)\gamma^{2}=\pm\mathrm{i}(\lambda-\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}), we have

E~​(γ,ε)=E⁡(∓i​γ2+λbr,ε)\displaystyle\widetilde{E}(\gamma,\varepsilon)=E(\mp\mathrm{i}\gamma^{2}+\lambda_{\mathrm{br}},\varepsilon)

with γ≈0\gamma\approx 0, where the upper or lower sign is taken simultaneously, and refer to E~​(γ,ε)\widetilde{E}(\gamma,\varepsilon) as the extended Evans function. See Sections 4.3 and 4.4 for more details.

Here we compute the Evans function E⁡(λ,0)E(\lambda,0) for ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0}. The eigenvalue problem ℒ0​ψ=λ​ψ\mathscr{L}_{0}\psi=\lambda\psi is separated into three parts: (A) the first and second components

−p′′+ω​p−∂12F⁡(U0​(x)2,0)​U0​(x)2​(p+q)−∂1F⁡(U0​(x)2,0)​p=i​λ​p,−q′′+ω​q−∂12F⁡(U0​(x)2,0)​U0​(x)2​(p+q)−∂1F⁡(U0​(x)2,0)​q=−i​λ​q;\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &-p^{\prime\prime}+\omega p-\partial_{1}^{2}F(U_{0}(x)^{2},0)U_{0}(x)^{2}(p+q)-\partial_{1}F(U_{0}(x)^{2},0)p=\mathrm{i}\lambda p,\\ &-q^{\prime\prime}+\omega q-\partial_{1}^{2}F(U_{0}(x)^{2},0)U_{0}(x)^{2}(p+q)-\partial_{1}F(U_{0}(x)^{2},0)q=-\mathrm{i}\lambda q;\end{aligned} (2.10)

(B) the fourth component

−p′′+s​p−∂2F⁡(U0​(x)2,0,μ)​p=−i​λ​p;\displaystyle-p^{\prime\prime}+sp-\partial_{2}F(U_{0}(x)^{2},0;\mu)p=-\mathrm{i}\lambda p; (2.11)

and (C) the third component

−p′′+s​p−∂2F⁡(U0​(x)2,0,μ)​p=i​λ​p.\displaystyle-p^{\prime\prime}+sp-\partial_{2}F(U_{0}(x)^{2},0;\mu)p=\mathrm{i}\lambda p. (2.12)

Let (pj​(x,λ),qj​(x,λ))(p_{j}(x,\lambda),q_{j}(x,\lambda)), j=1,2,5,6j=1,2,5,6, denote the Jost solutions to (2.10) such that

limx→−∞|e−ν1​x​(p1​(x,λ)q1​(x,λ)p1′​(x,λ)q1′​(x,λ))−(10ν10)|=limx→−∞|e−ν2​x​(p2​(x,λ)q2​(x,λ)p2′​(x,λ)q2′​(x,λ))−(010ν2)|=limx→+∞|eν1​x​(p5​(x,λ)q5​(x,λ)p5′​(x,λ)q5′​(x,λ))−(10−ν10)|=limx→+∞|eν2​x​(p6​(x,λ)q6​(x,λ)p6′​(x,λ)q6′​(x,λ))−(010−ν2)|=0,\begin{split}&\lim_{x\to-\infty}\left\lvert\mathrm{e}^{-\nu_{1}x}\!\begin{pmatrix}p_{1}(x,\lambda)\\ q_{1}(x,\lambda)\\ p_{1}^{\prime}(x,\lambda)\\ q_{1}^{\prime}(x,\lambda)\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\\ \nu_{1}\\ 0\end{pmatrix}\right\rvert=\lim_{x\to-\infty}\left\lvert\mathrm{e}^{-\nu_{2}x}\!\begin{pmatrix}p_{2}(x,\lambda)\\ q_{2}(x,\lambda)\\ p_{2}^{\prime}(x,\lambda)\\ q_{2}^{\prime}(x,\lambda)\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 1\\ 0\\ \nu_{2}\end{pmatrix}\right\rvert\\ &=\lim_{x\to+\infty}\left\lvert\mathrm{e}^{\nu_{1}x}\!\begin{pmatrix}p_{5}(x,\lambda)\\ q_{5}(x,\lambda)\\ p_{5}^{\prime}(x,\lambda)\\ q_{5}^{\prime}(x,\lambda)\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\\ -\nu_{1}\\ 0\end{pmatrix}\right\rvert=\lim_{x\to+\infty}\left\lvert\mathrm{e}^{\nu_{2}x}\!\begin{pmatrix}p_{6}(x,\lambda)\\ q_{6}(x,\lambda)\\ p_{6}^{\prime}(x,\lambda)\\ q_{6}^{\prime}(x,\lambda)\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 1\\ 0\\ -\nu_{2}\end{pmatrix}\right\rvert=0,\end{split} (2.13)

where

ν1​(λ)=ω−i​λ,ν2​(λ)=ω+i​λ.\displaystyle\nu_{1}(\lambda)=\sqrt{\omega-\mathrm{i}\lambda},\quad\nu_{2}(\lambda)=\sqrt{\omega+\mathrm{i}\lambda}. (2.14)

Actually, by a fundamental result on linear differential equations (e.g., Section 3.8 of [9]), these solutions exist since (p,q)=(e±ν1​x,0)(p,q)=(e^{\pm\nu_{1}x},0) and (0,e±ν2​x)(0,e^{\pm\nu_{2}x}) are solutions to

−p′′+ω​p=i​λ​p,−q′′+ω​q=−i​λ​q,-p^{\prime\prime}+\omega p=\mathrm{i}\lambda p,\quad-q^{\prime\prime}+\omega q=-\mathrm{i}\lambda q,

to which (2.10) converges as x→±∞x\to\pm\infty. Moreover, one of (p1,q1)(p_{1},q_{1}) and (p2,q2)(p_{2},q_{2}) (resp. (p5,q5)(p_{5},q_{5}) and (p6,q6)(p_{6},q_{6})) is uniquely determined but the other is not, depending on which has a bigger real part, ν1\nu_{1} or ν2\nu_{2}. On the other hand, let p4​(x,λ)p_{4}(x,\lambda) and p8​(x,λ)p_{8}(x,\lambda) (resp. p3​(x,λ)p_{3}(x,\lambda) and p7​(x,λ)p_{7}(x,\lambda)) denote the Jost solutions to (2.11) (resp. to (2.12)) such that

limx→−∞|e−ν4​x​(p4​(x,λ)p4′​(x,λ))−(1ν4)|=limx→+∞|eν4​x​(p8​(x,λ)p8′​(x,λ))−(1−ν4)|=0\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty}\left\lvert\mathrm{e}^{-\nu_{4}x}\!\begin{pmatrix}p_{4}(x,\lambda)\\ p_{4}^{\prime}(x,\lambda)\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}1\\ \nu_{4}\end{pmatrix}\right\rvert=\lim_{x\to+\infty}\left\lvert\mathrm{e}^{\nu_{4}x}\!\begin{pmatrix}p_{8}(x,\lambda)\\ p_{8}^{\prime}(x,\lambda)\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -\nu_{4}\end{pmatrix}\right\rvert=0 (2.15)

(resp.

limx→−∞|e−ν3​x​(p3​(x,λ)p3′​(x,λ))−(1ν3)|=limx→+∞|eν3​x​(p7​(x,λ)p7′​(x,λ))−(1−ν3)|=0\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty}\left\lvert\mathrm{e}^{-\nu_{3}x}\!\begin{pmatrix}p_{3}(x,\lambda)\\ p_{3}^{\prime}(x,\lambda)\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}1\\ \nu_{3}\end{pmatrix}\right\rvert=\lim_{x\to+\infty}\left\lvert\mathrm{e}^{\nu_{3}x}\!\begin{pmatrix}p_{7}(x,\lambda)\\ p_{7}^{\prime}(x,\lambda)\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -\nu_{3}\end{pmatrix}\right\rvert=0 (2.16)

) and

p4​(x,λ)=p8​(−x,λ),p3​(x,λ)=p4​(x,−λ),p7​(x,λ)=p8​(x,−λ),\displaystyle p_{4}(x,\lambda)=p_{8}(-x,\lambda),\quad p_{3}(x,\lambda)=p_{4}(x,-\lambda),\quad p_{7}(x,\lambda)=p_{8}(x,-\lambda),

where

ν3​(λ)=s−i​λ,ν4​(λ)=s+i​λ.\displaystyle\nu_{3}(\lambda)=\sqrt{s-\mathrm{i}\lambda},\quad\nu_{4}(\lambda)=\sqrt{s+\mathrm{i}\lambda}. (2.17)

These solutions uniquely exist since p=e±ν4​xp=e^{\pm\nu_{4}x} (resp. p=e±ν3​xp=e^{\pm\nu_{3}x}) are solutions to

−p′′+s​p=i​λ​p(resp. −p′′+s​p=i​λ​q),-p^{\prime\prime}+sp=\mathrm{i}\lambda p\quad(\mbox{resp.\ }-p^{\prime\prime}+sp=\mathrm{i}\lambda q),

to which (2.11) (resp. (2.12)) converges as x→±∞x\to\pm\infty. See Section 5 for more details on the Jost solutions. We choose the branch cut for νj​(λ)\nu_{j}(\lambda), j=1,…,4j=1,\ldots,4, such that

−π<arg⁡(λ±i​ω),arg⁡(λ±i​s)<π,-\pi<\arg(\lambda\pm\mathrm{i}\omega),\arg(\lambda\pm\mathrm{i}s)<\pi,

i.e.,

−3​π4<arg⁡ν1​(λ),arg⁡ν3​(λ)<π4,−π4<arg⁡ν2​(λ),arg⁡ν4​(λ)<3​π4.\displaystyle-\frac{3\pi}{4}<\arg\nu_{1}(\lambda),\arg\nu_{3}(\lambda)<\frac{\pi}{4},\quad-\frac{\pi}{4}<\arg\nu_{2}(\lambda),\arg\nu_{4}(\lambda)<\frac{3\pi}{4}. (2.18)

We refer to λ=±i​ω\lambda=\pm\mathrm{i}\omega and ±i​s\pm\mathrm{i}s as the branch points.

We now obtain the Evans function for ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0} as

E⁡(λ,0)=EA​(λ)​EB​(λ)​EC​(λ),\displaystyle E(\lambda,0)=E_{\mathrm{A}}(\lambda)E_{\mathrm{B}}(\lambda)E_{\mathrm{C}}(\lambda), (2.19)

where

EA​(λ)⋅⋅=det(p1p2p5p6q1q2q5q6p1′p2′p5′p6′q1′q2′q5′q6′)⁡(0,λ),\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{A}}(\lambda)\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}\hss}\raisebox{-1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}}=\det\!\begin{pmatrix}p_{1}&p_{2}&p_{5}&p_{6}\\ q_{1}&q_{2}&q_{5}&q_{6}\\ p_{1}^{\prime}&p_{2}^{\prime}&p_{5}^{\prime}&p_{6}^{\prime}\\ q_{1}^{\prime}&q_{2}^{\prime}&q_{5}^{\prime}&q_{6}^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}\!(0,\lambda), (2.20)
EB​(λ)⋅⋅=det(p4p8p4′p8′)⁡(0,λ),\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{B}}(\lambda)\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}\hss}\raisebox{-1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}}=\det\!\begin{pmatrix}p_{4}&p_{8}\\ p_{4}^{\prime}&p_{8}^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}\!(0,\lambda), (2.21)

and

EC​(λ)⋅⋅=det(p3p7p3′p7′)⁡(0,λ).\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{C}}(\lambda)\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}\hss}\raisebox{-1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}}=\det\!\begin{pmatrix}p_{3}&p_{7}\\ p_{3}^{\prime}&p_{7}^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}\!(0,\lambda). (2.22)

Near the branch points λ=λbr∈{±i​ω,±i​s}\lambda=\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}\in\{\pm\mathrm{i}\omega,\pm\mathrm{i}s\}, by γ2=±i⁡(λ−λbr)\gamma^{2}=\pm\mathrm{i}(\lambda-\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}), we also modify (2.19) to

E~​(γ,0)=E~A​(γ)​E~B​(γ)​E~C​(γ)\displaystyle\widetilde{E}(\gamma,0)=\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{A}}(\gamma)\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{B}}(\gamma)\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{C}}(\gamma)

with γ≈0\gamma\approx 0, where E~​(γ,0)\widetilde{E}(\gamma,0) is the extended Evans function for ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0} and

E~A,B,C​(γ)=EA,B,C​(∓i​γ2+λbr).\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{A,B,C}}(\gamma)=E_{\mathrm{A,B,C}}(\mp\mathrm{i}\gamma^{2}+\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}).

Here the upper or lower sign has been taken simultaneously.

Let λ0∈i​ℝ∖{0}\lambda_{0}\in\mathrm{i}\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} be a zero of E⁡(λ,0)E(\lambda,0). Since p3​(x,λ)=p4​(x,−λ)p_{3}(x,\lambda)=p_{4}(x,-\lambda), p7​(x,λ)=p8​(x,−λ)p_{7}(x,\lambda)=p_{8}(x,-\lambda), we have EC​(λ)=EB​(−λ)E_{\mathrm{C}}(\lambda)=E_{\mathrm{B}}(-\lambda). From the Sturm-Liouville theory (see, e.g., Section 2.3.2 of [20]) we see that (2.11) has only a finite number of eigenvalues, all of which are simple and belong to i⁡(−∞,s)\mathrm{i}(-\infty,s). So we only have to consider zeros on i⁡(−∞,s)\mathrm{i}(-\infty,s) for EB​(λ)E_{\mathrm{B}}(\lambda) since eigenvalues of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} related to them remain near the segment for ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small. Under this observation, we see that the following six cases occur:

  1. (I)

    λ0∈i⁡(−min⁡{ω,s},min⁡{ω,s})\lambda_{0}\in\mathrm{i}(-\min\{\omega,s\},\min\{\omega,s\});

  2. (II)

    λ0=±i​min⁡{ω,s}\lambda_{0}=\pm\mathrm{i}\min\{\omega,s\};

  3. (III)

    λ0\lambda_{0} is a zero of EB​(λ)E_{\mathrm{B}}(\lambda) and belongs to i⁡(ω,s)\mathrm{i}(\omega,s) when ω<s\omega<s;

  4. (IV)

    λ0\lambda_{0} is a zero of EB​(λ)E_{\mathrm{B}}(\lambda) and belongs to i⁡(−∞,−min⁡{ω,s})\mathrm{i}(-\infty,-\min\{\omega,s\});

  5. (V)

    λ0=i​s\lambda_{0}=\mathrm{i}s is a zero of EB​(λ)E_{\mathrm{B}}(\lambda) when ω<s\omega<s;

  6. (VI)

    λ0=±i​ω\lambda_{0}=\pm\mathrm{i}\omega is a zero of EA​(λ)E_{\mathrm{A}}(\lambda) when s<ωs<\omega.

In cases (I) and (II) λ0\lambda_{0} is a zero of either EA​(λ)E_{\mathrm{A}}(\lambda), EB​(λ)E_{\mathrm{B}}(\lambda), or EC​(λ)E_{\mathrm{C}}(\lambda). We can restate cases (III)-(V) with EC​(λ)E_{\mathrm{C}}(\lambda) as

  1. (III’)

    λ0\lambda_{0} is a zero of EC​(λ)E_{\mathrm{C}}(\lambda) and belongs to i⁡(−s,−ω)\mathrm{i}(-s,-\omega) when ω<s\omega<s;

  2. (IV’)

    λ0\lambda_{0} is a zero of EC​(λ)E_{\mathrm{C}}(\lambda) and belongs to i⁡(min⁡{ω,s},∞)\mathrm{i}(\min\{\omega,s\},\infty);

  3. (V’)

    λ0=−i​s\lambda_{0}=-\mathrm{i}s is a zero of EC​(λ)E_{\mathrm{C}}(\lambda) when ω<s\omega<s.

Obviously, λ0\lambda_{0} is an isolated eigenvalue of ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0} in case (I), while it is an endpoint of σess​(ℒ0)\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathscr{L}_{0}) in case (II). For the other cases λ0\lambda_{0} is not an endpoint of σess​(ℒ0)\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathscr{L}_{0}) and it is an embedded eigenvalue or a resonance pole of ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0}. Actually, λ0\lambda_{0} is a resonance pole in cases (V) and (VI). In the following, we state our results in these six cases separately. Proofs of the results are provided in Section 6 except for one of Proposition 2.7. For simplicity, we essentially assume that λ0\lambda_{0} is a simple zero of E⁡(λ,0)E(\lambda,0) in cases (I), (III), and (IV). In cases (II), (V), and (VI), we treat the extended Evans function E~​(γ,0)\widetilde{E}(\gamma,0), and assume that its zero γ=0\gamma=0 is simple. If these assumptions do not hold, then more complicated analyses are required to determine the fate of the eigenvalue λ0\lambda_{0} when ε>0\varepsilon>0. Note that the zero λ=0\lambda=0 of E⁡(λ,0)E(\lambda,0) is not simple by the symmetry (1.4) and (1.5) but the dimension of the generalized kernel of ℒ\mathscr{L} does not change after the pitchfork bifurcations, as stated at the end of Section 4.1. Hence, the zero λ=0\lambda=0 does not cause the spectral instability of bifurcated solitary waves.

We begin with case (I).

Proposition 2.7.

Suppose that the hypotheses of Theorem 2.2 hold and λ=λ0∈i⁡(−min⁡{ω,s},min⁡{ω,s})\lambda=\lambda_{0}\in\mathrm{i}(-\min\{\omega,s\},\min\{\omega,s\}) is a simple zero of E⁡(λ,0)E(\lambda,0). Then there exists an eigenvalue of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} close to λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0} on the imaginary axis for ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small.

Proof.

The statement of this proposition immediately follows from the symmetry of σ⁡(ℒε)\sigma(\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon}). ∎

For case (II) we have the following (see Section 6.2 for its proof).

Theorem 2.8.

Suppose that the hypotheses of Theorem 2.2 hold, λ0=i​min⁡{ω,s}\lambda_{0}=\mathrm{i}\min\{\omega,s\} (resp. λ0=−i​min⁡{ω,s}\lambda_{0}=-\mathrm{i}\min\{\omega,s\}) is a zero of E⁡(λ,0)E(\lambda,0), and γ=0\gamma=0 is a simple zero of E~​(γ,0)\widetilde{E}(\gamma,0) with λbr=λ0\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}=\lambda_{0}. Then for ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small, one of the following three cases occurs:

  1. (i)

    ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} has a unique simple eigenvalue in λ0+i⁡(−∞,0)\lambda_{0}+\mathrm{i}(-\infty,0) (resp. λ0+i⁡(0,∞)\lambda_{0}+\mathrm{i}(0,\infty)) and no resonance pole near λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0};

  2. (ii)

    ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} has a unique resonance pole in λ0+i⁡(−∞,0)\lambda_{0}+\mathrm{i}(-\infty,0) (resp. λ0+i⁡(0,∞)\lambda_{0}+\mathrm{i}(0,\infty)) and no eigenvalue near λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0};

  3. (iii)

    λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0} remains as an eigenvalue or a resonance pole of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon}.

We turn to case (III) and assume that ω<s\omega<s and EB​(λ0)=0E_{\mathrm{B}}(\lambda_{0})=0 for λ0∈i⁡(ω,s)\lambda_{0}\in\mathrm{i}(\omega,s). Define

Δj​(λ)⋅⋅=pj​(0,λ)​pj′​(0,λ)+qj​(0,λ)​qj′​(0,λ),\displaystyle\Delta_{j}(\lambda)\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}\hss}\raisebox{-1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}}=p_{j}(0,\lambda)p_{j}^{\prime}(0,\lambda)+q_{j}(0,\lambda)q_{j}^{\prime}(0,\lambda), (2.23)
ℐj​(λ)⋅⋅=∫−∞∞∂1∂2F⁡(U0​(x)2,0,0)​U0​(x)​V1​(x)​(pj​(x,λ)+qj​(x,λ))​p4​(x,λ)​𝑑x\displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{j}(\lambda)\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}\hss}\raisebox{-1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\partial_{1}\partial_{2}F(U_{0}(x)^{2},0;0)U_{0}(x)V_{1}(x)\bigl(p_{j}(x,\lambda)+q_{j}(x,\lambda)\bigr)p_{4}(x,\lambda)\,\mathrm{d}x (2.24)

for j=1,2j=1,2. We note that (p1,q1)(p_{1},q_{1}) is uniquely determined when λ0∈i⁡(ω,s)\lambda_{0}\in\mathrm{i}(\omega,s) and that (p2,q2)(p_{2},q_{2}) is also uniquely determined by Lemma 6.2 below if Δ1​(λ0)≠0\Delta_{1}(\lambda_{0})\neq 0. We have the following result (see Section 6.3 for its proof).

Theorem 2.9.

Let ω<s\omega<s. Suppose that the hypotheses of Theorem 2.2 hold, λ0∈i⁡(ω,s)\lambda_{0}\in\mathrm{i}(\omega,s) is a simple zero of EB​(λ)E_{\mathrm{B}}(\lambda) with EA​(λ0),EC​(λ0)≠0E_{\mathrm{A}}(\lambda_{0}),E_{\mathrm{C}}(\lambda_{0})\neq 0, and Δ1​(λ0),ℐ2​(λ0)≠0\Delta_{1}(\lambda_{0}),\mathcal{I}_{2}(\lambda_{0})\neq 0. Then for ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small, ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} has no eigenvalue in a neighborhood of λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0}.

Remark 2.10.

In Theorem 2.9, the neighborhood of λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0} can be taken independently of ε\varepsilon. This also holds in Theorems 2.13 and 2.14 below.

We next consider case (IV) partially and assume that EB​(λ0)=0E_{\mathrm{B}}(\lambda_{0})=0 for λ0∈i⁡(−∞,−ω)\lambda_{0}\in\mathrm{i}(-\infty,-\omega). So the case of s<ωs<\omega and λ0∈i[−ω,−s)\lambda_{0}\in\mathrm{i}[-\omega,-s) is excluded. As in case (III), (p2,q2)(p_{2},q_{2}) is uniquely determined when λ0∈i⁡(−∞,−min⁡{ω,s})\lambda_{0}\in\mathrm{i}(-\infty,-\min\{\omega,s\}) and that (p1,q1)(p_{1},q_{1}) is also uniquely determined by Lemma 6.2 below if Δ2​(λ0)≠0\Delta_{2}(\lambda_{0})\neq 0. We have the following result (see Section 6.4 for its proof).

Theorem 2.11.

Suppose that the hypotheses of Theorem 2.2 holds and λ0∈i⁡(−∞,−ω)\lambda_{0}\in\mathrm{i}(-\infty,-\omega) is a simple zero of EB​(λ)E_{\mathrm{B}}(\lambda) with EA​(λ0),EC​(λ0)≠0E_{\mathrm{A}}(\lambda_{0}),E_{\mathrm{C}}(\lambda_{0})\neq 0, and Δ2​(λ0),ℐ1​(λ0)≠0\Delta_{2}(\lambda_{0}),\mathcal{I}_{1}(\lambda_{0})\neq 0. Then for ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small, ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} has an eigenvalue with a positive real part in an O⁡(ε2)O(\varepsilon^{2})-neighborhood of λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0}.

Remark 2.12.

Assume that s<ωs<\omega and λ0∈i[−ω,−s)\lambda_{0}\in\mathrm{i}[-\omega,-s). Then we have Re​λ​(ε)=O⁡(ε3)\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda(\varepsilon)=O(\varepsilon^{3}), as shown in Remark 6.8 below, where λ⁡(ε)\lambda(\varepsilon) is the eigenvalue of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} near λ0\lambda_{0}. Hence, more tremendous treatments than those in the proof of Theorem 2.11 are required to estimate an eigenvalue of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} near λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0} for ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small. This situation does not occur for the cubic nonlinearity (1.2) even if s<ωs<\omega as seen in Section 7.

For case (V) we have the following (see Section 6.5 for its proof).

Theorem 2.13.

Let ω<s\omega<s. Suppose that the hypotheses of Theorem 2.2 hold, EB​(i​s)=0E_{\mathrm{B}}(\mathrm{i}s)=0, γ=0\gamma=0 is a simple zero of E~B​(γ)\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{B}}(\gamma) with λbr=i​s\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}=\mathrm{i}s with EA​(i​s),EC​(i​s)≠0E_{\mathrm{A}}(\mathrm{i}s),E_{\mathrm{C}}(\mathrm{i}s)\neq 0 and Δ1​(i​s),ℐ2​(i​s)≠0\Delta_{1}(\mathrm{i}s),\mathcal{I}_{2}(\mathrm{i}s)\neq 0. Then for ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small, ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} has no eigenvalue in a neighborhood of λ=i​s\lambda=\mathrm{i}s and no resonance pole at λ=i​s\lambda=\mathrm{i}s.

Finally we consider case (VI) and assume that s<ωs<\omega. We make the following assumption.

  • (A4)

    There exists a bounded solution (p^​(x),q^​(x))(\hat{p}(x),\hat{q}(x)) to (2.10) with λ=i​ω\lambda=\mathrm{i}\omega such that

    limx→±∞p^​(x)=0,limx→−∞q^​(x)≠0,limx→+∞q^​(x)≠0.\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\hat{p}(x)=0,\quad\lim_{x\to-\infty}\hat{q}(x)\neq 0,\quad\lim_{x\to+\infty}\hat{q}(x)\neq 0.

An equivalent statement to (A4) is given in Remark 6.11 below. We have the following result (see Section 6.6 for its proof).

Theorem 2.14.

Let s<ωs<\omega. Suppose that the hypotheses of Theorem 2.2 hold, EA​(i​ω)=0E_{\mathrm{A}}(\mathrm{i}\omega)=0, γ=0\gamma=0 is a simple zero of E~A​(γ)\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{A}}(\gamma) with λbr=i​ω\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}=i\omega and EB​(i​ω),EC​(i​ω)≠0E_{\mathrm{B}}(\mathrm{i}\omega),E_{\mathrm{C}}(\mathrm{i}\omega)\neq 0, and Δ1​(i​ω)≠0\Delta_{1}(\mathrm{i}\omega)\neq 0. Then, under assumption (A4), ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} has no eigenvalue in a neighborhood of λ=±i​ω\lambda=\pm\mathrm{i}\omega and no resonance pole at λ=±i​ω\lambda=\pm\mathrm{i}\omega for ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small.

Remark 2.15.

Let λ0∈i​ℝ\lambda_{0}\in\mathrm{i}\mathbb{R} be a simple eigenvalue of ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0} which is a zero of EB​(λ)E_{\mathrm{B}}(\lambda). We see that λ0\lambda_{0} has a positive (resp. negative) Krein signature if it belongs to the upper (resp. lower) half plane (see Remark 5.2 below). See Section 7.1 of [20] or Section 4.2 for the definition of the Krein signature. Note that a similar statement is also found in Section 3.1 of [31]. It follows from Theorems 2.9, 2.13, and 2.14 that embedded eigenvalues of ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0} with positive Krein signatures as well as resonance poles at the endpoint of σess​(ℒ0)\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathscr{L}_{0}) disappear when ε>0\varepsilon>0, provided that Δ1​(λ0),ℐ2​(λ0)≠0\Delta_{1}(\lambda_{0}),\mathcal{I}_{2}(\lambda_{0})\neq 0. On the other hand, Theorem 2.11 states that embedded eigenvalues of ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0} with negative Krein signatures have nonzero real parts when ε>0\varepsilon>0, provided that Δ2​(λ0),ℐ1​(λ0)≠0\Delta_{2}(\lambda_{0}),\mathcal{I}_{1}(\lambda_{0})\neq 0. These claims completely agree with the generic results obtained by Pelinovsky and Yang [31] and Cuccagna et al. [10] stated in Section 1.

3. Bifurcations and Approximate Homoclinic Solutions

In this section, we review the Melnikov analysis of [6] in a sufficient setting for our purpose and prove Theorem 2.2 by applying it to (1.6).

3.1. Melnikov Analysis

We begin with the Melnikov analysis of [6] on pitchfork bifurcations of homoclinic orbits in a class of two-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian systems. Our setting is simpler but sufficient for the analysis of (1.6) in Section 3.2.

Consider two-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian systems of the form

ξ′=J​Dξ​H​(ξ,η,μ)T,η′=J​Dη​H​(ξ,η,μ)T,(ξ,η)∈ℝ2×ℝ2,\xi^{\prime}=J\mathrm{D}_{\xi}H(\xi,\eta;\mu)^{\mathrm{T}},\quad\eta^{\prime}=J\mathrm{D}_{\eta}H(\xi,\eta;\mu)^{\mathrm{T}},\quad(\xi,\eta)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\times\mathbb{R}^{2}, (3.1)

where the Hamiltonian function H:ℝ2×ℝ2×ℝ→ℝH:\mathbb{R}^{2}\times\mathbb{R}^{2}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is Cr+1C^{r+1} (r≥4r\geq 4), the superscript ‘T’ represents the transpose operator and JJ is the 2×22\times 2 symplectic matrix given by

J=(01−10).J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}.

We make the following assumptions.

  • (M1)

    Dξ​H​(0,0,μ)=Dη​H​(0,0,μ)=0\mathrm{D}_{\xi}H(0,0;\mu)=\mathrm{D}_{\eta}H(0,0;\mu)=0 for any μ∈ℝ\mu\in\mathbb{R}.

  • (M2)

    Dη​H​(ξ,0,0)=0\mathrm{D}_{\eta}H(\xi,0;0)=0 for any ξ∈ℝ2\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2}.

(M1) means that the origin (ξ,η)=(0,0)(=O)(\xi,\eta)=(0,0)\,(=O) is an equilibrium of (3.1) for any μ∈ℝ\mu\in\mathbb{R}, and (M2) means that the ξ\xi-plane, {(ξ,η)∣η=0}\{(\xi,\eta)\mid\eta=0\}, is invariant under the flow of (3.1) at μ=0\mu=0. In particular, the system of (3.1) restricted on the ξ\xi-plane at μ=0\mu=0,

ξ′=J​Dξ​H​(ξ,0,0)T,\xi^{\prime}=J\mathrm{D}_{\xi}H(\xi,0;0)^{\mathrm{T}}, (3.2)

has an equilibrium at ξ=0\xi=0. Moreover, Dξj​Dη​H​(ξ,0,0)=0\mathrm{D}_{\xi}^{j}\mathrm{D}_{\eta}H(\xi,0;0)=0, j=1,2,…j=1,2,\ldots, for any ξ∈ℝ2\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2}.

  • (M3)

    At μ=0\mu=0 the equilibrium ξ=0\xi=0 in (3.2) is a hyperbolic saddle, i.e., J​Dξ2​H​(0,0,0)J\mathrm{D}_{\xi}^{2}H(0,0;0) has a pair of positive and negative real eigenvalues ±λ1\pm\lambda_{1} (λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0), and has a homoclinic orbit ξh​(x)\xi^{\mathrm{h}}(x).

  • (M4)

    J​Dη2​H​(0,0,0)J\mathrm{D}_{\eta}^{2}H(0,0;0) has a pair of positive and negative real eigenvalues ±λ2\pm\lambda_{2} (λ2>0\lambda_{2}>0).

(M3) and (M4) mean that the equilibrium OO is a hyperbolic saddle in (3.1) and has a homoclinic orbit (ξ,η)=(ξh​(x),0)(\xi,\eta)=(\xi^{\mathrm{h}}(x),0). The hyperbolic saddle OO has two-dimensional stable and unstable manifolds which intersect along the homoclinic orbit (ξh​(x),0)(\xi^{\mathrm{h}}(x),0).

The variational equation (VE) of (3.1) around the homoclinic orbit (ξh​(x),0)(\xi^{\mathrm{h}}(x),0) at μ=0\mu=0 is given by

δ​ξ′=J​Dξ2​H​(ξh​(x),0,0)​δ​ξ,δ​η′=J​Dη2​H​(ξh​(x),0,0)​δ​η.\delta\xi^{\prime}=J\mathrm{D}_{\xi}^{2}H(\xi^{\mathrm{h}}(x),0;0)\delta\xi,\quad\delta\eta^{\prime}=J\mathrm{D}_{\eta}^{2}H(\xi^{\mathrm{h}}(x),0;0)\delta\eta. (3.3)

The first equation of (3.3) has a nonzero bounded solution δξ=ξh′(x)\delta\xi=\xi^{\mathrm{h}\prime}(x) satisfying limx→±∞δ​ξ​(x)=0\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\delta\xi(x)=0, where ξh′(x)=dd​xξh(x)\xi^{\mathrm{h}\prime}(x)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\xi^{\mathrm{h}}(x). We assume the following.

  • (M5)

    The second equation of (3.3) also has a nonzero bounded solution δ​η=ϕ⁡(x)\delta\eta=\phi(x) such that limx→±∞ϕ⁡(x)=0\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\phi(x)=0.

When (3.1) is analytic, it was shown in [6] that the VE (3.3) is integrable in the meaning of differential Galois theory [32] if (M5) holds.

The adjoint equation for (3.3), which we call the adjoint variational equation (AVE), is given by

δ​ξ^′=Dξ2​H​(ξh​(x),0,0)​J​δ​ξ^,δ​η^′=Dη2​H​(ξh​(x),0,0)​J​δ​η^\delta\hat{\xi}^{\prime}=\mathrm{D}_{\xi}^{2}H(\xi^{\mathrm{h}}(x),0;0)J\delta\hat{\xi},\quad\delta\hat{\eta}^{\prime}=\mathrm{D}_{\eta}^{2}H(\xi^{\mathrm{h}}(x),0;0)J\delta\hat{\eta} (3.4)

since Dξ2​H​(ξh​(x),0,0),Dη2​H​(ξh​(x),0,0)\mathrm{D}_{\xi}^{2}H(\xi^{\mathrm{h}}(x),0;0),\mathrm{D}_{\eta}^{2}H(\xi^{\mathrm{h}}(x),0;0) are symmetric matrices and JT=−JJ^{\mathrm{T}}=-J. Hence, δξ^=−Jξh′(x)=DξH(ξh(x),0)\delta\hat{\xi}=-J\xi^{\mathrm{h}\prime}(x)=\mathrm{D}_{\xi}H(\xi^{\mathrm{h}}(x),0) and δ​η^=−J​ϕ​(x)\delta\hat{\eta}=-J\phi(x) are, respectively, nonzero bounded solutions of the first and second equations of (3.4) since J2=−I2J^{2}=-I_{2} and J−1=−JJ^{-1}=-J, where InI_{n} is the n×nn\times n identity matrix.

We also assume that the Hamiltonian system (3.1) is ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-equivariant.

  • (M6)

    There exist two 2×22\times 2 matrices S1,S2S_{1},S_{2}, such that either S1≠I2S_{1}\neq I_{2} or S2≠I2S_{2}\neq I_{2}, Sj2=I2S_{j}^{2}=I_{2}, j=1,2j=1,2, and

    S1​J​Dξ​H​(ξ,η,μ)T=J​Dξ​H​(S1​ξ,S2​η,μ)T,\displaystyle S_{1}J\mathrm{D}_{\xi}H(\xi,\eta;\mu)^{\mathrm{T}}=J\mathrm{D}_{\xi}H(S_{1}\xi,S_{2}\eta;\mu)^{\mathrm{T}},
    S2​J​Dη​H​(ξ,η,μ)T=J​Dη​H​(S1​ξ,S2​η,μ)T.\displaystyle S_{2}J\mathrm{D}_{\eta}H(\xi,\eta;\mu)^{\mathrm{T}}=J\mathrm{D}_{\eta}H(S_{1}\xi,S_{2}\eta;\mu)^{\mathrm{T}}.

It follows from (M6) that if (ξ,η)=(ξ¯​(x),η¯​(x))(\xi,\eta)=(\bar{\xi}(x),\bar{\eta}(x)) is a solution to (3.1), then so is (ξ,η)=(S1​ξ¯​(x),S2​η¯​(x))(\xi,\eta)=(S_{1}\bar{\xi}(x),S_{2}\bar{\eta}(x)). See, e.g., Section 7.4 of [22] for more details on ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-equivariant systems. In particular, the space ℝ4\mathbb{R}^{4} can be decomposed into a direct sum as

ℝ4=X+⊕X−,\mathbb{R}^{4}=X^{+}\oplus X^{-},

where X±={(ξ,η)∈ℝ4∣(S1​ξ,S2​η)=±(ξ,η)}X^{\pm}=\{(\xi,\eta)\in\mathbb{R}^{4}\mid(S_{1}\xi,S_{2}\eta)=\pm(\xi,\eta)\}. Under (M6), if (ξh​(x),0)∈X+(\xi^{\mathrm{h}}(x),0)\in X^{+} for any x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, then the VE (3.3) and AVE (3.4) are also ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-equivariant since

S1​J​Dξ2​H​(ξ,η,μ)=J​Dξ2​H​(S1​ξ,S2​η,μ)​S1,\displaystyle S_{1}J\mathrm{D}_{\xi}^{2}H(\xi,\eta;\mu)=J\mathrm{D}_{\xi}^{2}H(S_{1}\xi,S_{2}\eta;\mu)S_{1},

for any ξ,η∈ℝ2\xi,\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. Finally, we assume the following.

  • (M7)

Let

Theorem 3.1.

Under (M1)-(M7), suppose that a¯2,b¯2≠0\bar{a}_{2},\bar{b}_{2}\neq 0. Then a pitchfork bifurcation of homoclinic orbits occurs at μ=0\mu=0. Moreover, it is supercritical or subcritical, depending on whether a¯2​b¯2<0\bar{a}_{2}\bar{b}_{2}<0 or >0>0.

See [6] for the proof of Theorem 3.1. More general nn-dimensional systems (n≥4n\geq 4) containing non-Hamiltonian systems and saddle-node bifurcations of homoclinic orbits were treated there. Similar results were recently obtained for reversible systems in [36].

Remark 3.2.

Homoclinic orbits created at the pitchfork bifurcation detected by Theorem 3.1 are written as

(ξ,η)=(ξh​(x),α​ϕ​(x))+O⁡(α2),\displaystyle(\xi,\eta)=(\xi^{\mathrm{h}}(x),\alpha\phi(x))+O(\alpha^{2}),

where α\alpha is a small parameter satisfying

up to O⁡(α8+μ4)O(\sqrt{\alpha^{8}+\mu^{4}}). See [6] for the details.

4. Hamiltonian-Krein Index and Evans Function

In this section, we present the two main tools used in the next two sections, the Hamiltonian-Krein index theory and Evans function technique, for the stability problem of solitary waves of the form

(u,v)=(ei​ω​t​U​(x,ω,s),ei​s​t​V​(x,ω,s))\displaystyle(u,v)=(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}U(x;\omega,s),\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}st}V(x;\omega,s)) (4.1)

in the CNLS equations (1.1), to which (1.3) reduces when c,x0,θ,ϕ=0c,x_{0},\theta,\phi=0 as stated in Section 1. Here (U,V)=(U⁡(x,ω,s),V⁡(x,ω,s))(U,V)=(U(x;\omega,s),V(x;\omega,s)) is a homoclinic solution to (1.6) such that U⁡(x,ω,s),V⁡(x,ω,s)→0U(x;\omega,s),V(x;\omega,s)\to 0 as x→±∞x\to\pm\infty, where its dependence on ω,s\omega,s is explicitly provided although it will be frequently dropped below. We also fix the value of μ\mu and suppress the dependence of FF and (U,V)(U,V) on μ\mu. See [18, 19, 20, 30] for more details on these methods. We easily see that there exist positive constants ρ,C\rho,C such that

|U⁡(x)|+|V⁡(x)|≤C​e−ρ​|x|,x∈ℝ.\displaystyle|U(x)|+|V(x)|\leq C\mathrm{e}^{-\rho|x|},\quad x\in\mathbb{R}. (4.2)

4.1. Linearized Operator

We first rewrite (1.1) by means of (u,v)(u,v) and their complex conjugates (w,z)⋅⋅=(u∗,v∗)(w,z)\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}\hss}\raisebox{-1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}}=(u^{*},v^{*}) as

i∂tu+∂x2u+∂1F(uw,vz)u=0,i∂tv+∂x2v+∂2F(uw,vz)v=0,i∂tw−∂x2w−∂1F(uw,vz)w=0,i∂tz−∂x2z−∂2F(uw,vz)z=0,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{i}\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}^{2}u+\partial_{1}F(uw,vz)u=0,\quad\mathrm{i}\partial_{t}v+\partial_{x}^{2}v+\partial_{2}F(uw,vz)v=0,\\ &\mathrm{i}\partial_{t}w-\partial_{x}^{2}w-\partial_{1}F(uw,vz)w=0,\quad\mathrm{i}\partial_{t}z-\partial_{x}^{2}z-\partial_{2}F(uw,vz)z=0,\end{aligned} (4.3)

in which the solitary wave (4.1) in (1.1) corresponds to

(u,w,v,z)=(ei​ω​t​U​(x),e−i​ω​t​U​(x),ei​s​t​V​(x),e−i​s​t​V​(x)).\displaystyle(u,w,v,z)=(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}U(x),\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\omega t}U(x),\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}st}V(x),\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}st}V(x)). (4.4)

Letting

u=ei​ω​t​(U⁡(x)+δ​ξ1),w=e−i​ω​t​(U⁡(x)+δ​ξ2),\displaystyle u=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}(U(x)+\delta\xi_{1}),\quad w=\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\omega t}(U(x)+\delta\xi_{2}),
v=ei​s​t​(V⁡(x)+δ​ξ3),z=e−i​s​t​(V⁡(x)+δ​ξ4),\displaystyle v=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}st}(V(x)+\delta\xi_{3}),\quad z=\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}st}(V(x)+\delta\xi_{4}),

we obtain the linearized problem for (4.3) around the solitary wave (4.4) as

∂tδ​ξ=ℒ​δ​ξ,\displaystyle\partial_{t}\delta\xi=\mathscr{L}\delta\xi,

where δ​ξ=(δ​ξ1,…,δ​ξ4)T\delta\xi=(\delta\xi_{1},\ldots,\delta\xi_{4})^{\mathrm{T}} and the linearized operator ℒ\mathscr{L} is given by (2.9). Substituting the separated variables ansatz δ​ξ​(t,x)=eλ​t​ψ​(x)\delta\xi(t,x)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\psi(x) into the above linearized problem yields the eigenvalue problem in a standard form,

ℒ​ψ=λ​ψ,ψ=(ψ1,…,ψ4)T.\displaystyle\mathscr{L}\psi=\lambda\psi,\quad\psi=(\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{4})^{\mathrm{T}}. (4.5)

By the symmetries (1.4) and (1.5), Ker⁡ℒ\Ker\mathscr{L} contains

φ1​(x)=(∂xU⁡(x,ω,s),∂xU⁡(x,ω,s),∂xV⁡(x,ω,s),∂xV⁡(x,ω,s))T,φ2​(x)=(i​U​(x,ω,s),−i​U​(x,ω,s),0,0)T,φ3​(x)=(0,0,i​V​(x,ω,s),−i​V​(x,ω,s))T.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\varphi_{1}(x)=(\partial_{x}U(x;\omega,s),\partial_{x}U(x;\omega,s),\partial_{x}V(x;\omega,s),\partial_{x}V(x;\omega,s))^{\mathrm{T}},\\ &\varphi_{2}(x)=(\mathrm{i}U(x;\omega,s),-\mathrm{i}U(x;\omega,s),0,0)^{\mathrm{T}},\\ &\varphi_{3}(x)=(0,0,\mathrm{i}V(x;\omega,s),-\mathrm{i}V(x;\omega,s))^{\mathrm{T}}.\end{aligned} (4.6)

Moreover,

χ1(x)=(−ixU(x;ω,s)/2,ixU(x;ω,s)/2,−ixV(x;ω,s)/2,ixV(x;ω,s)/2)T,χ2​(x)=(∂ωU⁡(x,ω,s),∂ωU⁡(x,ω,s),∂ωV⁡(x,ω,s),∂ωV⁡(x,ω,s))T,χ3​(x)=(∂sU⁡(x,ω,s),∂sU⁡(x,ω,s),∂sV⁡(x,ω,s),∂sV⁡(x,ω,s))T\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\chi_{1}(x)=(-\mathrm{i}xU(x;\omega,s)/2,\mathrm{i}xU(x;\omega,s)/2,-\mathrm{i}xV(x;\omega,s)/2,\mathrm{i}xV(x;\omega,s)/2)^{\mathrm{T}},\\ &\chi_{2}(x)=(\partial_{\omega}U(x;\omega,s),\partial_{\omega}U(x;\omega,s),\partial_{\omega}V(x;\omega,s),\partial_{\omega}V(x;\omega,s))^{\mathrm{T}},\\ &\chi_{3}(x)=(\partial_{s}U(x;\omega,s),\partial_{s}U(x;\omega,s),\partial_{s}V(x;\omega,s),\partial_{s}V(x;\omega,s))^{\mathrm{T}}\end{aligned} (4.7)

satisfy ℒ​χj=φj\mathscr{L}\chi_{j}=\varphi_{j}, j=1,2,3j=1,2,3, whenever they exist. For the fundamental solitary wave (1.7), φ3​(x)\varphi_{3}(x) and χ3​(x)\chi_{3}(x) vanish since (U,V)=(U0​(x),0)(U,V)=(U_{0}(x),0). Moreover, by (A3), ψ=(0,0,V1​(x),0)T\psi=(0,0,V_{1}(x),0)^{\mathrm{T}} and (0,0,0,V1​(x))T(0,0,0,V_{1}(x))^{\mathrm{T}} are contained in Ker⁡ℒ\Ker\mathscr{L} at μ=0\mu=0. Hence, dimgKer⁡ℒ\dim\gKer\mathscr{L} for the bifurcated solitary waves does not change after the pitchfork bifurcations detected by Theorem 2.2.

4.2. Hamiltonian-Krein Index

We introduce the transformation

ψ↦((ψ1+ψ2)/2,(ψ3+ψ4)/2,(ψ1−ψ2)/2​i,(ψ3−ψ4)/2​i)T.\displaystyle\psi\mapsto((\psi_{1}+\psi_{2})/2,(\psi_{3}+\psi_{4})/2,(\psi_{1}-\psi_{2})/2\mathrm{i},(\psi_{3}-\psi_{4})/2\mathrm{i})^{\mathrm{T}}. (4.8)

Under this transformation, the eigenvalue problem (4.5) is rewritten as

𝒥​ℒ​ψ=λ​ψ,ψ=(ψ1,…,ψ4)T,\displaystyle\mathcal{J}\mathcal{L}\psi=\lambda\psi,\quad\psi=(\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{4})^{\mathrm{T}}, (4.9)

where

𝒥=(O2I2−I2O2),ℒ=(ℒ+O2O2ℒ−)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}=\begin{pmatrix}O_{2}&I_{2}\\ -I_{2}&O_{2}\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathcal{L}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{L}_{+}&O_{2}\\ O_{2}&\mathcal{L}_{-}\end{pmatrix} (4.10)

with

ℒ−=(−∂x2+ω−∂1F(U2,V2)00−∂x2+s−∂2F(U2,V2)),ℒ+=ℒ−−(2​∂12F⁡(U2,V2)​U22​∂1∂2F⁡(U2,V2)​U​V2​∂1∂2F⁡(U2,V2)​U​V2​∂22F⁡(U2,V2)​V2).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\mathcal{L}_{-}=\begin{pmatrix}-\partial_{x}^{2}+\omega-\partial_{1}F(U^{2},V^{2})&0\\ 0&-\partial_{x}^{2}+s-\partial_{2}F(U^{2},V^{2})\end{pmatrix},\\ &\mathcal{L}_{+}=\mathcal{L}_{-}-\begin{pmatrix}2\partial_{1}^{2}F(U^{2},V^{2})U^{2}&2\partial_{1}\partial_{2}F(U^{2},V^{2})UV\\ 2\partial_{1}\partial_{2}F(U^{2},V^{2})UV&2\partial_{2}^{2}F(U^{2},V^{2})V^{2}\end{pmatrix}.\\ \end{aligned} (4.11)

We easily see that the spectrum does not change under this transformation. Moreover, (4.6) and (4.7) are transformed into

(U′​(x),V′​(x),0,0)T,(0,0,U⁡(x),0)T,(0,0,0,V⁡(x))T.\displaystyle(U^{\prime}(x),V^{\prime}(x),0,0)^{\mathrm{T}},\quad(0,0,U(x),0)^{\mathrm{T}},\quad(0,0,0,V(x))^{\mathrm{T}}.

and

(0,0,−xU(x)/2,−xV(x)/2)T,(∂ωU(x),∂ωV(x),0,0)T,(∂sU(x),∂sV(x),0,0)T,\displaystyle(0,0,-xU(x)/2,-xV(x)/2)^{\mathrm{T}},\ \ (\partial_{\omega}U(x),\partial_{\omega}V(x),0,0)^{\mathrm{T}},\ \ (\partial_{s}U(x),\partial_{s}V(x),0,0)^{\mathrm{T}},

respectively. Let ℒ±i​j\mathcal{L}_{\pm ij} be the (i,j)(i,j)-components of ℒ±\mathcal{L}_{\pm} for i,j=1,2i,j=1,2. Note that (A3) holds if and only if ℒ±22\mathcal{L}_{\pm 22} for the fundamental solitary wave (1.7) have a nontrivial kernel.

Define a 3×33\times 3 real matrix DD with entries

Di​j⋅⋅=⟨χi,i​Σ3​φj⟩L2=⟨χi,i​Σ3​ℒ​χj⟩L2\displaystyle D_{ij}\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}\hss}\raisebox{-1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}}=\langle\chi_{i},\mathrm{i}\Sigma_{3}\varphi_{j}\rangle_{L^{2}}=\langle\chi_{i},\mathrm{i}\Sigma_{3}\mathscr{L}\chi_{j}\rangle_{L^{2}}

for i,j=1,2,3i,j=1,2,3, i.e.,

D=((‖U‖L22+‖V‖L22)/2000−∂ω∥U∥L22−∂ω∥V∥L220−∂s∥U∥L22−∂s∥V∥L22).\displaystyle D=\begin{pmatrix}(\|U\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|V\|_{L^{2}}^{2})/2&0&0\\ 0&-\partial_{\omega}\|U\|_{L^{2}}^{2}&-\partial_{\omega}\|V\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\\ 0&-\partial_{s}\|U\|_{L^{2}}^{2}&-\partial_{s}\|V\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\end{pmatrix}. (4.12)

Since i​Σ3​ℒ\mathrm{i}\Sigma_{3}\mathscr{L} is self-adjoint, we see that DD is symmetric, so that ∂ω‖V‖L22=∂s‖U‖L22\partial_{\omega}\|V\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=\partial_{s}\|U\|_{L^{2}}^{2}. Let n⁡(𝒜)\mathrm{n}(\mathcal{A}) denote the number of negative eigenvalues for a self-adjoint operator 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

Definition 4.1.

Let krk_{\mathrm{r}} be the number of real positive eigenvalues of 𝒥​ℒ\mathcal{J}\mathcal{L}, and let kck_{\mathrm{c}} be the number of its complex eigenvalues in the first open quadrant of ℂ\mathbb{C}. Let HλH^{\lambda} be the linear map induced by the bilinear form ⟨v,ℒ​w⟩L2\langle v,\mathcal{L}w\rangle_{L^{2}} restricted to the generalized eigenspace gKer⁡(𝒥​ℒ−λ)\gKer(\mathcal{J}\mathcal{L}-\lambda), and let ki−k_{\mathrm{i}}^{-} be the sum of n⁡(Hλ)\mathrm{n}(H^{\lambda}) when λ\lambda runs through all purely imaginary eigenvalues of 𝒥​ℒ\mathcal{J}\mathcal{L} with positive imaginary parts. Then the sum KHam=kr+2​kc+2​ki−K_{\mathrm{Ham}}=k_{\mathrm{r}}+2k_{\mathrm{c}}+2k_{\mathrm{i}}^{-} is called the Hamiltonian-Krein index. Moreover, a purely imaginary, nonzero eigenvalue λ\lambda of 𝒥​ℒ\mathcal{J}\mathcal{L} is said to have a positive ((resp. negative)) Krein signature if HλH^{\lambda} is positive ((resp. negative)) definite on gKer⁡(𝒥​ℒ−λ)\gKer(\mathcal{J}\mathcal{L}-\lambda).

We have the following theorem, which is frequently referred to as the index theorem.

Theorem 4.2 (Kapitula et al. [18, 19], Pelinovsky [30]).

If DD is nonsingular, then KHam=n⁡(ℒ)−n⁡(D)K_{\mathrm{Ham}}=\mathrm{n}(\mathcal{L})-\mathrm{n}(D).

Using Theorem 4.2 and the Stability and Instability Theorems of [16] (see also [20]), we obtain the following result.

Theorem 4.3.

Suppose that DD is nonsingular. If KHam=0K_{\mathrm{Ham}}=0 (resp. KHamK_{\mathrm{Ham}} is odd), then the solitary wave (4.1) is orbitally stable (resp. unstable).

Remark 4.4.

For the fundamental solitary wave (1.7) we have φ3​(x),χ3​(x)≡0\varphi_{3}(x),\chi_{3}(x)\equiv 0. Replacing (4.12) with

D=(‖U0‖L22/200−∂ω∥U0∥L22),\displaystyle D=\begin{pmatrix}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}/2&0\\ 0&-\partial_{\omega}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\end{pmatrix}, (4.13)

the statements of Theorems 4.2 and 4.3 also hold for (1.7).

4.3. Evans Functions

We rewrite the eigenvalue problem (4.5) as a system of first-order ODEs,

Y′=A⁡(x,λ)​Y,\displaystyle Y^{\prime}=A(x,\lambda)Y, (4.14)

where Y=(ψ1,…,ψ4,ψ1′,…,ψ4′)TY=(\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{4},\psi_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,\psi_{4}^{\prime})^{\mathrm{T}}. Define

A∞​(λ)⋅⋅=limx→±∞A⁡(x,λ)=(O4I4ω−i​λ0000ω+i​λ0000s−i​λ0000s+i​λO4).\displaystyle A_{\infty}(\lambda)\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}\hss}\raisebox{-1.29167pt}{$\cdot$}}=\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}A(x,\lambda)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c|c}O_{4}&I_{4}\\ \hline\cr\begin{matrix}\omega-\mathrm{i}\lambda&0&0&0\\ 0&\omega+\mathrm{i}\lambda&0&0\\ 0&0&s-\mathrm{i}\lambda&0\\ 0&0&0&s+\mathrm{i}\lambda\end{matrix}&O_{4}\end{array}\right).

The matrix A∞​(λ)A_{\infty}(\lambda) has eigenvalues given by (2.14), (2.17), and

νj+4(λ)=−νj(λ),j=1,…,4.\nu_{j+4}(\lambda)=-\nu_{j}(\lambda),\quad j=1,\ldots,4.

Let

Ω=Ω1∩Ω2∩Ω3∩Ω4,\displaystyle\Omega=\Omega_{1}\cap\Omega_{2}\cap\Omega_{3}\cap\Omega_{4},

where

Ω1={λ∈ℂ∣Re​λ>0​or​Im​λ>−ω},Ω2={λ∈ℂ∣Re​λ>0​or​Im​λ<ω},Ω3={λ∈ℂ∣Re​λ>0​or​Im​λ>−s},Ω4={λ∈ℂ∣Re​λ>0​or​Im​λ<s},\begin{split}&\Omega_{1}=\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\mid\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda>0\ \text{or}\ \mathrm{Im}\,\lambda>-\omega\},\\ &\Omega_{2}=\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\mid\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda>0\ \text{or}\ \mathrm{Im}\,\lambda<\omega\},\\ &\Omega_{3}=\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\mid\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda>0\ \text{or}\ \mathrm{Im}\,\lambda>-s\},\\ &\Omega_{4}=\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\mid\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda>0\ \text{or}\ \mathrm{Im}\,\lambda<s\},\end{split} (4.17)

and let

Ω^=ℂ∖{λ∈ℂ∣Re​λ≤0​and​Im​λ∈{±ω,±s}}.\displaystyle\widehat{\Omega}=\mathbb{C}\setminus\{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\mid\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda\leq 0\ \text{and}\ \mathrm{Im}\,\lambda\in\{\pm\omega,\pm s\}\}.

Note that νj​(λ)\nu_{j}(\lambda), j=1,…,4j=1,\ldots,4, are analytic in Ω^\widehat{\Omega}, by the definition of their branch cut (2.18). Moreover, νj​(λ)\nu_{j}(\lambda) (resp. νj+4​(λ)\nu_{j+4}(\lambda)) has a positive (resp. negative) real part in Ωj\Omega_{j} for j=1,…,4j=1,\ldots,4. Let

Ωe={λ∈Ω^|min1≤j≤4⁡Re​νj​(λ)>−ρ2},\displaystyle\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}=\left\{\lambda\in\widehat{\Omega}\;\middle|\;\min_{1\leq j\leq 4}\mathrm{Re}\,\nu_{j}(\lambda)>-\frac{\rho}{2}\right\}, (4.18)

which is an open neighborhood of Ω\Omega in Ω^\widehat{\Omega}, where ρ\rho is given in (4.2). The regions Ω\Omega and Ωe\Omega_{\mathrm{e}} are displayed as the shaded areas in Figs. 1 (a) and (b), respectively. We have the following lemma (see, e.g., Theorem 9.2.3 of [20] and Proposition 1.2 of [29], for the proof).

Lemma 4.5.

One can take an eigenvector vj​(λ)v_{j}(\lambda) of A∞​(λ)A_{\infty}(\lambda) for the eigenvalue νj​(λ)\nu_{j}(\lambda) such that it is analytic in Ωe\Omega_{\mathrm{e}} and continuous at the branch points λ=±i​ω,±i​s\lambda=\pm\mathrm{i}\omega,\pm\mathrm{i}s for j=1,…,8j=1,\ldots,8. Moreover, for j=1,…,8j=1,\ldots,8, there exist two solutions Yj±​(x,λ)Y_{j}^{\pm}(x,\lambda) to (4.14) and a positive constant Cj​(λ)C_{j}(\lambda) such that

|e−νj​(λ)​xYj−(x,λ)−vj(λ)|≤Cj(λ)e−ρ|x|/2as x→−∞,|e−νj​(λ)​xYj+(x,λ)−vj(λ)|≤Cj(λ)e−ρ|x|/2as x→+∞,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &|\mathrm{e}^{-\nu_{j}(\lambda)x}Y_{j}^{-}(x,\lambda)-v_{j}(\lambda)|\leq C_{j}(\lambda)\mathrm{e}^{-\rho|x|/2}&\text{as $x\to-\infty$},\\ &|\mathrm{e}^{-\nu_{j}(\lambda)x}Y_{j}^{+}(x,\lambda)-v_{j}(\lambda)|\leq C_{j}(\lambda)\mathrm{e}^{-\rho|x|/2}&\text{as $x\to+\infty$},\end{aligned} (4.19)

and Yj±​(x,λ)Y_{j}^{\pm}(x,\lambda) are analytic with respect to λ∈Ωe\lambda\in\Omega_{\mathrm{e}} and continuous at the branch points for any fixed x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, where Cj​(λ)C_{j}(\lambda) is bounded on any compact subset of Ωe\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}.

We refer to Yj±​(x,λ)Y_{j}^{\pm}(x,\lambda), j=1,…,8j=1,\ldots,8, as the Jost solutions for (4.14). Note that for (4.14), both of Yj−​(x,λ)Y_{j}^{-}(x,\lambda), j=1,…,4j=1,\ldots,4, and Yj+​(x,λ)Y_{j}^{+}(x,\lambda), j=5,…,8j=5,\ldots,8, give bases of the spaces of solutions which decay as x→−∞x\to-\infty and x→+∞x\to+\infty, respectively, when λ∈Ω\lambda\in\Omega. We define the Evans function E⁡(λ)E(\lambda) for the eigenvalue problem (4.5) as

E⁡(λ)=det(Y1−​Y2−​Y3−​Y4−​Y5+​Y6+​Y7+​Y8+)​(x,λ),\displaystyle E(\lambda)=\det\bigl(Y_{1}^{-}\;\;Y_{2}^{-}\;\;Y_{3}^{-}\;\;Y_{4}^{-}\;\;Y_{5}^{+}\;\;Y_{6}^{+}\;\;Y_{7}^{+}\;\;Y_{8}^{+}\bigr)(x,\lambda), (4.20)

when λ∈Ωe∪{±i​ω,±i​s}\lambda\in\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}\cup\{\pm\mathrm{i}\omega,\pm\mathrm{i}s\}. Since tr⁡A⁡(x,λ)=0\trace A(x,\lambda)=0, the right hand side of (4.20) is independent of xx. Although the Jost solutions are not uniquely determined in general, we easily see that zeros of E⁡(λ)E(\lambda) do not depend on a particular choice of them. We have the following fundamental properties of the Evans function (see, e.g., Theorem 10.2.2 of [20], for the proof).

Proposition 4.6.

The Evans function E⁡(λ)E(\lambda) is analytic in Ωe\Omega_{\mathrm{e}} and continuous at the branch points λ=±i​ω,±i​s\lambda=\pm\mathrm{i}\omega,\pm\mathrm{i}s. When λ0∈Ω∪σess​(ℒ)\lambda_{0}\in\Omega\cup\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathscr{L}), it is sufficient for E⁡(λ0)=0E(\lambda_{0})=0 that λ0\lambda_{0} is an eigenvalue of ℒ\mathscr{L}. When λ0∈Ω\lambda_{0}\in\Omega, the condition is also necessary. Moreover, the algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalue equals the multiplicity dd of the zero for E⁡(λ)E(\lambda), for which

E⁡(λ0)=∂λE⁡(λ0)=⋯=∂λd−1E⁡(λ0)=0,∂λdE⁡(λ0)≠0.\displaystyle E(\lambda_{0})=\partial_{\lambda}E(\lambda_{0})=\cdots=\partial_{\lambda}^{d-1}E(\lambda_{0})=0,\quad\partial_{\lambda}^{d}E(\lambda_{0})\neq 0.

Note that the Evans function E⁡(λ)E(\lambda) may not be analytic at the branch points. Near the branch points, we modify the Evans function as follows. Let λbr=i​ω\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}=\mathrm{i}\omega or i​s\mathrm{i}s. Substituting the relation λ=λbr−i​γ2\lambda=\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}-\mathrm{i}\gamma^{2} into (4.14), we have

Y′=A⁡(x,λbr−i​γ2)​Y.\displaystyle Y^{\prime}=A(x,\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}-\mathrm{i}\gamma^{2})Y.

All eigenvalues of A∞​(λbr−i​γ2)A_{\infty}(\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}-\mathrm{i}\gamma^{2}) are analytic near γ=0\gamma=0. We use γ\gamma instead of λ\lambda and apply the above arguments to obtain the Jost solutions and Evans function. We write this Evans function as E~​(γ)\widetilde{E}(\gamma) near γ=0\gamma=0 and call it the extended Evans function. Especially, E~​(γ)\widetilde{E}(\gamma) is analytic on a Riemann surface that is a two-sheeted cover of ℂ\mathbb{C}. For λbr=−i​ω\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}=-\mathrm{i}\omega or −i​s-\mathrm{i}s, using the transformation γ2=−i⁡(λ−λbr)\gamma^{2}=-\mathrm{i}(\lambda-\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}), we define the extended Evans function similarly. So we immediately obtain the following proposition.

Proposition 4.7.

The extended Evans function E~​(γ)\widetilde{E}(\gamma) is analytic near γ=0\gamma=0. Let λbr=i​ω\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}=\mathrm{i}\omega or i​s\mathrm{i}s. Suppose that λ=λbr−i​γ2∈Ωe\lambda=\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}-\mathrm{i}\gamma^{2}\in\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}. Then it is necessary and sufficient for E⁡(λ)=0E(\lambda)=0 that E~​(γ)=0\widetilde{E}(\gamma)=0 and −π/4<argγ<3π/4-\pi/4<\arg\gamma<3\pi/4. Moreover, if λ=λbr−i​γ2∈Ω\lambda=\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}-\mathrm{i}\gamma^{2}\in\Omega, then the condition is also necessary and sufficient for λ\lambda to be an eigenvalue of ℒ\mathscr{L}. For λbr=−i​ω\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}=-\mathrm{i}\omega or −i​s-\mathrm{i}s, similar statements also hold.

We easily see that (4.5) has a bounded non-decaying solution only if λ∈σess​(ℒ)\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathscr{L}) is a resonance pole.

4.4. Parameter-Dependent Solitary Waves

We now consider the case in which the homoclinic solution to (1.6) smoothly depends on a small parameter ε\varepsilon and write the linearized operator ℒ\mathscr{L} as ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon}. Let E⁡(λ,ε)E(\lambda,\varepsilon) and E~​(γ,ε)\widetilde{E}(\gamma,\varepsilon), respectively, denote the original and extended Evans functions. From Propositions 4.6 and 4.7 we obtain the following.

Proposition 4.8.

Suppose that the Evans function E⁡(λ,0)E(\lambda,0) has a simple zero at λ=λ0∈Ωe\lambda=\lambda_{0}\in\Omega_{\mathrm{e}}. Then there exists a unique smooth function λ⁡(ε)\lambda(\varepsilon) near ε=0\varepsilon=0 such that E⁡(λ⁡(ε),ε)=0E(\lambda(\varepsilon),\varepsilon)=0 and λ⁡(0)=λ0\lambda(0)=\lambda_{0}. Moreover,

If λ⁡(ε)∈Ω\lambda(\varepsilon)\in\Omega, then it is an eigenvalue of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon}.

Proof.

Applying the implicit function theorem to E⁡(λ,ε)=0E(\lambda,\varepsilon)=0, we obtain the first and second parts. The last part immediately follows from Proposition 4.6. ∎

Proposition 4.9.

Let λbr=i​ω\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}=\mathrm{i}\omega or i​s\mathrm{i}s (resp. −i​ω-\mathrm{i}\omega or −i​s-\mathrm{i}s). Suppose that E~​(γ,0)\widetilde{E}(\gamma,0) has a simple zero at γ=0\gamma=0. Then there exists a unique smooth function γ⁡(ε)\gamma(\varepsilon) near ε=0\varepsilon=0 such that E~​(γ​(ε),ε)=0\widetilde{E}(\gamma(\varepsilon),\varepsilon)=0 and γ⁡(0)=0\gamma(0)=0. Moreover,

∂εγ⁡(0)=−∂εE~​(0,0)∂γE~​(0,0),∂ε2γ⁡(0)=−∂γ2E~​(0,0)​∂εγ​(0)2+2​∂γ∂εE~​(0,0)​∂εγ⁡(0)+∂ε2E~​(0,0)∂γE~​(0,0).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\partial_{\varepsilon}\gamma(0)=-\frac{\partial_{\varepsilon}\widetilde{E}(0,0)}{\partial_{\gamma}\widetilde{E}(0,0)},\\ &\partial_{\varepsilon}^{2}\gamma(0)=-\frac{\partial_{\gamma}^{2}\widetilde{E}(0,0)\partial_{\varepsilon}\gamma(0)^{2}+2\partial_{\gamma}\partial_{\varepsilon}\widetilde{E}(0,0)\partial_{\varepsilon}\gamma(0)+\partial_{\varepsilon}^{2}\widetilde{E}(0,0)}{\partial_{\gamma}\widetilde{E}(0,0)}.\end{aligned} (4.22)

If Re​γ​(ε)>0\mathrm{Re}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)>0 and Im​γ​(ε)≥0\mathrm{Im}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)\geq 0 (resp. Re​γ​(ε)>0\mathrm{Re}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)>0 and Im​γ​(ε)≤0\mathrm{Im}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)\leq 0), then λbr−i​γ​(ε)2\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}-\mathrm{i}\gamma(\varepsilon)^{2} (resp. λbr+i​γ​(ε)2\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}+\mathrm{i}\gamma(\varepsilon)^{2}) is a zero of E⁡(λ,ε)E(\lambda,\varepsilon). Especially, if Re​γ​(ε)>0\mathrm{Re}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)>0 and Im​γ​(ε)>0\mathrm{Im}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)>0 (resp. Re​γ​(ε)>0\mathrm{Re}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)>0 and Im​γ​(ε)<0\mathrm{Im}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)<0), then the zero is an eigenvalue of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} with a positive real part. If Re​γ​(ε)<0\mathrm{Re}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)<0 or Im​γ​(ε)<0\mathrm{Im}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)<0 (resp. Re​γ​(ε)<0\mathrm{Re}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)<0 or Im​γ​(ε)>0\mathrm{Im}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)>0), then ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} has no eigenvalue near λ=λbr\lambda=\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}.

Proof.

The first and second parts immediately follow from the implicit function theorem. Let λbr=i​ω\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}=\mathrm{i}\omega or i​s\mathrm{i}s and let λ⁡(ε)=λbr−i​γ​(ε)2\lambda(\varepsilon)=\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}-\mathrm{i}\gamma(\varepsilon)^{2}. We prove the remaining parts. Since Re​λ​(ε)=2​Re​γ​(ε)​Im​γ​(ε)\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda(\varepsilon)=2\,\mathrm{Re}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)\,\mathrm{Im}\,\gamma(\varepsilon) and Im​λ​(ε)=Im​λbr−(Re​γ​(ε))2+(Im​γ​(ε))2\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda(\varepsilon)=\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}-(\mathrm{Re}\,\gamma(\varepsilon))^{2}+(\mathrm{Im}\,\gamma(\varepsilon))^{2}, we see that if Re​γ​(ε)>0\mathrm{Re}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)>0 and Im​γ​(ε)≥0\mathrm{Im}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)\geq 0, then λ⁡(ε)\lambda(\varepsilon) is a zero of E⁡(λ,ε)E(\lambda,\varepsilon) by Proposition 4.7. On the other hand, assume that Re​γ​(ε)<0\mathrm{Re}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)<0 or Im​γ​(ε)<0\mathrm{Im}\,\gamma(\varepsilon)<0 and that ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} has an eigenvalue λ1​(ε)\lambda_{1}(\varepsilon) near λ=λbr\lambda=\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}. By the symmetry of σ⁡(ℒε)\sigma(\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon}), we can assume Re​λ1​(ε)≥0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_{1}(\varepsilon)\geq 0. Then λ1​(ε)\lambda_{1}(\varepsilon) is a zero of E⁡(λ,ε)E(\lambda,\varepsilon) by Proposition 4.6. However, E⁡(λ,ε)E(\lambda,\varepsilon) does not have such a zero by Proposition 4.7. This yields a contradiction so that ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} has no eigenvalue near λ=λbr\lambda=\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}. Thus, we complete the proof. ∎

As stated in Section 2, the eigenvalue problem (4.5) is separated into three parts: (A) the first and second components; (B) the fourth component; and (C) the third component. (A)

The first and second components of (4.5) become (2.10), which are the same as the well-understood eigenvalue problem for u=ei​ω​t​U0​(x)u=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}U_{0}(x) in the single nonlinear Schrödinger equation with the nonlinearity ∂1F⁡(|u|2,0)​u\partial_{1}F(|u|^{2},0)u. We summarize fundamental spectral properties of (2.10) as follows (see, e.g., Section 5.3.1 of [39] for the proof).

All eigenvalues of (2.10) are either real or purely imaginary. Moreover, (2.10) has a pair of positive and negative eigenvalues with the same modulus if ∂ω‖U0‖L22<0\partial_{\omega}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}<0 and has no nonzero real eigenvalues if ∂ω‖U0‖L22>0\partial_{\omega}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}>0.

(B)

The fourth component of (4.5) becomes (2.11). Let pjp_{j}, j=4,8j=4,8, be the Jost solutions (2.11) satisfying (2.15), as in Section 2.2. Proof of Theorem 2.5.

From the above arguments in parts (A), (B), and (C) we see that all eigenvalues of ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0} are either real or purely imaginary. Moreover, by Proposition 5.1, the number of positive eigenvalues of ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0} is zero or one, so that the fundamental solitary wave (1.7) is spectrally stable or unstable, depending on whether ∂ω‖U0‖L22\partial_{\omega}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2} is positive or negative.

6. Spectral Stability of the Bifurcated Solitary Waves

We next consider the bifurcated solitary waves (2.5) near μ=0\mu=0 and give the remaining proofs of the main results in Section 2 by using the techniques of Section 4.

6.1. Proof of Theorem 2.6

We begin with the following direct consequence of the Hamiltonian-Krein index theory described in Section 4.

Proposition 6.1.

Let ℓ\ell be the number of zeros of V1​(x)V_{1}(x). For ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small, the Hamiltonian-Krein index for the bifurcated solitary waves (2.5) are given by KHam=kr+2​ℓK_{\mathrm{Ham}}=k_{\mathrm{r}}+2\ell, where kr=0k_{\mathrm{r}}=0 if ∂ω‖U0‖L22>0\partial_{\omega}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}>0 and kr=1k_{\mathrm{r}}=1 if ∂ω‖U0‖L22<0\partial_{\omega}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}<0.

Proof.

Let ℒ±\mathcal{L}_{\pm} and DD be given by (4.11) and (4.12), respectively, for the bifurcated solitary wave (2.5). By the Sturm-Liouville theory and the standard perturbation argument, we have

n⁡(ℒ−)=ℓ,n⁡(ℒ+)={ℓ+1if b¯2>0;ℓ+2if b¯2<0\displaystyle\mathrm{n}(\mathcal{L}_{-})=\ell,\qquad\mathrm{n}(\mathcal{L}_{+})=\begin{cases}\ell+1&\text{if $\bar{b}_{2}>0$};\\ \ell+2&\text{if $\bar{b}_{2}<0$}\end{cases}

(see Section 3.1 of [31] and Section 6.1 of [20] for details). On the other hand, substituting (2.6) into (4.12) and using the symmetry of DD, we compute

D22=−∂ω∥U0∥L22+4​⟨U0,U2⟩L22b¯2+O(ε2),\displaystyle D_{22}=-\partial_{\omega}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\frac{4\langle U_{0},U_{2}\rangle_{L^{2}}^{2}}{\bar{b}_{2}}+O(\varepsilon^{2}),
D23=D32=2​⟨U0,U2⟩L2​‖V1‖L22b¯2+O⁡(ε2),D33=‖V1‖L24b¯2+O⁡(ε2).\displaystyle D_{23}=D_{32}=\frac{2\langle U_{0},U_{2}\rangle_{L^{2}}\|V_{1}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}}{\bar{b}_{2}}+O(\varepsilon^{2}),\quad D_{33}=\frac{\|V_{1}\|_{L^{2}}^{4}}{\bar{b}_{2}}+O(\varepsilon^{2}).

Thus, n⁡(D)\mathrm{n}(D) equals the number of negative elements in the set {−∂ω∥U0∥L22,b¯2}\{-\partial_{\omega}\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2},\bar{b}_{2}\}. Hence, KHam=n⁡(ℒ−)+n⁡(ℒ+)−n⁡(D)=kr+2​ℓK_{\mathrm{Ham}}=\mathrm{n}(\mathcal{L}_{-})+\mathrm{n}(\mathcal{L}_{+})-\mathrm{n}(D)=k_{\mathrm{r}}+2\ell by Theorem 4.2. This completes the proof. ∎

Proof of Theorem 2.6.

Using Theorem 4.3 and Proposition 6.1, we immediately obtain the desired result. ∎

6.2. Proof of Theorem 2.8

We consider case (II) in Section 2.2.

Proof of Theorem 2.8.

Let λbr=i​min⁡{ω,s}\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}=\mathrm{i}\min\{\omega,s\} and let E~​(γ,ε)\widetilde{E}(\gamma,\varepsilon) denote the extended Evans function near the branch point λbr\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}, where γ2=i⁡(λ−λbr)\gamma^{2}=\mathrm{i}(\lambda-\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}), as in Section 4.4. For any γ,ε∈ℝ\gamma,\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R} near (γ,ε)=(0,0)(\gamma,\varepsilon)=(0,0), we can choose the ℝ\mathbb{R}-valued Jost solutions Yj±​(x,λ,ε)Y_{j}^{\pm}(x,\lambda,\varepsilon), j=1,…,8j=1,\ldots,8, since νj​(λ)=νj​(λbr−i​γ2)∈ℝ\nu_{j}(\lambda)=\nu_{j}(\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}-\mathrm{i}\gamma^{2})\in\mathbb{R}, j=1,…,8j=1,\ldots,8. For this choice we have E~​(γ,ε)∈ℝ\widetilde{E}(\gamma,\varepsilon)\in\mathbb{R}. Assume that γ=0\gamma=0 is a simple zero of E~​(γ,0)\widetilde{E}(\gamma,0). Using the implicit function theorem, we obtain a unique zero γ⁡(ε)∈ℝ\gamma(\varepsilon)\in\mathbb{R} of E~​(γ,ε)\widetilde{E}(\gamma,\varepsilon) with γ⁡(0)=0\gamma(0)=0. Using Proposition 4.9, we see that one of the following three cases occurs.

  1. (i)

    If γ⁡(ε)>0\gamma(\varepsilon)>0, then there exists a unique simple eigenvalue of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} near λbr\lambda_{\mathrm{br}} and ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} has no resonance pole near λbr\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}. The unique eigenvalue belongs to λbr+i⁡(−∞,0)\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}+\mathrm{i}(-\infty,0).

  2. (ii)

    If γ⁡(ε)<0\gamma(\varepsilon)<0, then there exists a unique resonance pole of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} near λbr\lambda_{\mathrm{br}} and ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} has no eigenvalue near λbr\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}. The unique resonance pole belongs to λbr+i⁡(−∞,0)\lambda_{\mathrm{br}}+\mathrm{i}(-\infty,0).

  3. (iii)

    If γ⁡(ε)=0\gamma(\varepsilon)=0, then λbr\lambda_{\mathrm{br}} remains as an eigenvalue or a resonance pole of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon}.

This completes the proof. ∎

Remark 6.11.

(A4) holds if and only if there exists a bounded solution (p^​(x),q^​(x))∉L2​(ℝ)×L2​(ℝ)(\hat{p}(x),\hat{q}(x))\not\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R})\times L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) to (2.10) with λ=i​ω\lambda=\mathrm{i}\omega. The necessity is obvious. Conversely, by Lemma 4.5 any bounded solution (p^​(x),q^​(x))(\hat{p}(x),\hat{q}(x)) to (2.10) with λ=i​ω\lambda=\mathrm{i}\omega satisfies one of the following asymptotics:

  1. (i)

    limx→±∞p^​(x)=0,limx→−∞q^​(x)=0,limx→+∞q^​(x)=0,\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\hat{p}(x)=0,\quad\lim_{x\to-\infty}\hat{q}(x)=0,\quad\lim_{x\to+\infty}\hat{q}(x)=0,

  2. (ii)

    limx→±∞p^​(x)=0,limx→−∞q^​(x)=0,limx→+∞q^​(x)≠0,\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\hat{p}(x)=0,\quad\lim_{x\to-\infty}\hat{q}(x)=0,\quad\lim_{x\to+\infty}\hat{q}(x)\neq 0,

  3. (iii)

    limx→±∞p^​(x)=0,limx→−∞q^​(x)≠0,limx→+∞q^​(x)=0,\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\hat{p}(x)=0,\quad\lim_{x\to-\infty}\hat{q}(x)\neq 0,\quad\lim_{x\to+\infty}\hat{q}(x)=0,

  4. (iv)

    limx→±∞p^​(x)=0,limx→−∞q^​(x)≠0,limx→+∞q^​(x)≠0.\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\hat{p}(x)=0,\quad\lim_{x\to-\infty}\hat{q}(x)\neq 0,\quad\lim_{x\to+\infty}\hat{q}(x)\neq 0.

If case (ii) or (iii) holds, then (p^​(−x),q^​(−x))(\hat{p}(-x),\hat{q}(-x)) is also a solution to (2.10) with λ=i​ω\lambda=\mathrm{i}\omega which is linearly independent of (p^​(x),q^​(x))(\hat{p}(x),\hat{q}(x)). Since the zero γ=0\gamma=0 of E~A​(γ)\widetilde{E}_{\mathrm{A}}(\gamma) is simple, we see that only case (i) or (iv) occurs. Hence, if (p^​(x),q^​(x))∉L2​(ℝ)×L2​(ℝ)(\hat{p}(x),\hat{q}(x))\not\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R})\times L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) then case (iv) must occur.

7. Example: Coupled Cubic Nonlinear Schrödinger Equations

In this section we apply the theories of Section 2 to the CNLS equations (1.1) with the particular nonlinearity (1.2), i.e.,

i​∂tu+∂x2u+(|u|2+β1​|v|2)​u=0,i​∂tv+∂x2v+(β1​|u|2+β2​|v|2)​v=0,\displaystyle\mathrm{i}\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}^{2}u+(|u|^{2}+\beta_{1}|v|^{2})u=0,\quad\mathrm{i}\partial_{t}v+\partial_{x}^{2}v+(\beta_{1}|u|^{2}+\beta_{2}|v|^{2})v=0, (7.1)

and illustrate the theoretical results with some numerical computations. Here we take β1∈ℝ\beta_{1}\in\mathbb{R} as the control parameter. Throughout this section, we set ω=1\omega=1 by replacing ω​t\omega t and s/ωs/\omega with tt and ss, respectively, if necessary without loss of generality.

Theorem 7.1.

For ℓ∈ℤ≥0\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, a pitchfork bifurcation of the fundamental solitary wave (1.7) with U0​(x)=2​sech⁡xU_{0}(x)=\sqrt{2}\sech x occurs at β1=β1(ℓ)\beta_{1}=\beta_{1}^{(\ell)} given by (7.3) if b¯2≠0\bar{b}_{2}\neq 0. In addition, it is supercritical or subcritical, depending on whether b¯2>0\bar{b}_{2}>0 or <0<0. Moreover, the bifurcated solitary waves are expressed as (2.5) with (2.6), where ε>0\varepsilon>0 is a small parameter such that β1=β1(ℓ)+O⁡(ε2)\beta_{1}=\beta_{1}^{(\ell)}+O(\varepsilon^{2}).

In what follows, we obtain tractable expressions for a¯2\bar{a}_{2} and b¯2\bar{b}_{2}. We begin with two auxiliary results.

Lemma 7.2.

We have

(−ℓ)jj!=(−1)j​(ℓj),\displaystyle\frac{(-\ell)_{j}}{j!}=(-1)^{j}\begin{pmatrix}\ell\\ j\end{pmatrix},

Let

Further computation of b¯2\bar{b}_{2} are carried out and its closed-form expressions for ℓ≤4\ell\leq 4 are given in Appendix B.

Figure 2(a) displays a numerically computed bifurcation diagram for homoclinic orbits in (3.9) for (ω,s,β2)=(1,4,2)(\omega,s,\beta_{2})=(1,4,2). Profiles of the homoclinic orbits on the first three bifurcation points at β1=12\beta_{1}=12 are plotted in Figs. 2(b) and (b). To obtain these results, we used a similar approach as in Section 5 of [6] and the computation tool AUTO [11]. We observe that pitchfork bifurcations occur at β1=3,6,10,15,21\beta_{1}=3,6,10,15,21 and they are supercritical except that the fifth one (ℓ=4\ell=4) is subcritical, as predicted by the theory (see also Fig. B.1(a)). Note that a pair of symmetric branches about V=0V=0 are born at each bifurcation point. Moreover, we see that a saddle-node bifurcation of the solitary waves on the fifth branches occurs at β1≈19.4\beta_{1}\approx 19.4 (more precisely, 19.41626​…19.41626\ldots). The VV-component of the homoclinic orbit on the (ℓ+1)(\ell+1)th branch have exactly ℓ\ell zeros for ℓ=0,1,2\ell=0,1,2. The details on the approach and further numerical results are given in [38].

7.2. Stability Analysis

We turn to the spectral stability of the fundamental and bifurcated solitary waves. For the fundamental solitary wave, noting that ‖U0‖L22=4​ω\|U_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=4\sqrt{\omega} for ω>0\omega>0 and applying Theorem 2.5, we immediately obtain the following result, which was also obtained in Remark 2.6 of [28] when β2=1\beta_{2}=1.

Theorem 7.5.

The fundamental solitary wave (1.7) with U0​(x)=2​sech⁡xU_{0}(x)=\sqrt{2}\sech x is orbitally and spectrally stable.

We next consider the bifurcated solitary waves (2.5) near β1=β1(ℓ)\beta_{1}=\beta_{1}^{(\ell)}. We first give some explicit expressions of the Jost solutions and Evans function for ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0} given in (5.1). The eigenvalue problem for ℒ0\mathscr{L}_{0} is separated into three parts as stated in Section 3.1.

(A)

(2.10) becomes

−p′′+p−2​sech2⁡x⁡(2​p+q)=i​λ​p,−q′′+q−2​sech2⁡x⁡(p+2​q)=−i​λ​q.\displaystyle-p^{\prime\prime}+p-2\sech^{2}x\,(2p+q)=\mathrm{i}\lambda p,\quad-q^{\prime\prime}+q-2\sech^{2}x\,(p+2q)=-\mathrm{i}\lambda q. (7.18)

The Jost solutions (pj,qj)(p_{j},q_{j}), j=1,2,5,6j=1,2,5,6, which satisfy our normalization conditions stated in Lemma 6.2, for (7.18) are explicitly given by

(p1​(x,λ)q1​(x,λ))=eν1​x(ν1+1)2((ν1−tanh⁡x)2−sech2⁡x),(p2​(x,λ)q2​(x,λ))=(q1​(x,−λ)p1​(x,−λ)),(pj+4​(x,λ)qj+4​(x,λ))=(pj​(−x,λ)qj​(−x,λ)),j=1,2,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\begin{pmatrix}p_{1}(x,\lambda)\\ q_{1}(x,\lambda)\end{pmatrix}=\frac{\mathrm{e}^{\nu_{1}x}}{(\nu_{1}+1)^{2}}\begin{pmatrix}(\nu_{1}-\tanh x)^{2}\\ -\sech^{2}x\end{pmatrix},\quad\begin{pmatrix}p_{2}(x,\lambda)\\ q_{2}(x,\lambda)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}q_{1}(x,-\lambda)\\ p_{1}(x,-\lambda)\end{pmatrix},\\ &\begin{pmatrix}p_{j+4}(x,\lambda)\\ q_{j+4}(x,\lambda)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}p_{j}(-x,\lambda)\\ q_{j}(-x,\lambda)\end{pmatrix},\quad j=1,2,\end{aligned} (7.19)

where ν1=ν1​(λ)\nu_{1}=\nu_{1}(\lambda) is given in (2.14) (see Section III of [21] and Section 10.4.1 of [20]). We compute the Evans function (2.20) for (7.18) as

EA​(λ)=4​ν1​(λ)​ν2​(λ)​(ν1​(λ)−1)2​(ν2​(λ)−1)2(ν1​(λ)+1)2​(ν2​(λ)+1)2\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{A}}(\lambda)=\frac{4\nu_{1}(\lambda)\nu_{2}(\lambda)(\nu_{1}(\lambda)-1)^{2}(\nu_{2}(\lambda)-1)^{2}}{(\nu_{1}(\lambda)+1)^{2}(\nu_{2}(\lambda)+1)^{2}}

This implies that (7.18) has only one eigenvalue λ=0\lambda=0 and it is of algebraic multiplicity four, and has resonance poles λ=±i\lambda=\pm\mathrm{i}.

(B)

(2.11) becomes
