  • (iii)

    Let s∈(0,1)s\in(0,1). We have

    ℐ(0)​(ν4​(i),ν2​(i))=−π​Γ​(1+i​ν)​Γ​(s+1+i​ν2)​Γ​(s+1−i​ν2)Γ⁡(s+1)​Γ​(s+2+i​ν2)​Γ​(−s+1+i​ν2),\displaystyle\mathcal{I}^{(0)}(\nu_{4}(\mathrm{i}),\nu_{2}(\mathrm{i}))=-\frac{\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(1+\mathrm{i}\nu)\Gamma\bigl(\frac{\sqrt{s}+1+\mathrm{i}\nu}{2}\bigr)\Gamma\bigl(\frac{\sqrt{s}+1-\mathrm{i}\nu}{2}\bigr)}{\Gamma(\sqrt{s}+1)\Gamma\bigl(\frac{\sqrt{s}+2+\mathrm{i}\nu}{2}\bigr)\Gamma\bigl(\frac{-\sqrt{s}+1+\mathrm{i}\nu}{2}\bigr)},

    where ν=1−s\nu=\sqrt{1-s}.

The proof of Lemma 7.10 is given in Appendix C.2. Using Proposition 7.8 and Lemma 7.10, we obtain the following theorem.

Theorem 7.11.

For each ℓ∈ℤ≥0\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, suppose that b¯2≠0\bar{b}_{2}\neq 0 and consider the solitary wave (2.5) bifurcated at β1=β1(ℓ)\beta_{1}=\beta_{1}^{(\ell)}. Let ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} be the linearized operator (2.9) with (1.2) around the bifurcated solitary waves.

  • (i)

    Let ℓ=0\ell=0. The bifurcated solitary waves are orbitally and spectrally stable. Moreover, for ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small, there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} has neither eigenvalues nor resonance poles except for {0}∪i⁡(−min⁡{1,s}−δ,−min⁡{1,s}+δ)∪i⁡(min⁡{1,s}−δ,min⁡{1,s}+δ)\{0\}\cup\mathrm{i}(-\min\{1,s\}-\delta,-\min\{1,s\}+\delta)\cup\mathrm{i}(\min\{1,s\}-\delta,\min\{1,s\}+\delta).

  • (ii)

    Let ℓ>0\ell>0. If

    s∉{−ℓ2+k22​(ℓ+k)|k∈{−⌊(2+1)​ℓ⌋,…,−ℓ−1}},\displaystyle\sqrt{s}\notin\left\{-\frac{\ell^{2}+k^{2}}{2(\ell+k)}\;\middle|\;k\in\{-\lfloor(\sqrt{2}+1)\ell\rfloor,\ldots,-\ell-1\}\right\},

    then for ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small, ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} has a pair of eigenvalues with positive and negative real parts near λ=±i​ℓ​(2​s+ℓ)\lambda=\pm\mathrm{i}\ell(2\sqrt{s}+\ell), i.e., the bifurcated solitary waves are spectrally unstable.

Proof.

The orbital and spectral stability of the bifurcated solitary waves with ℓ=0\ell=0 immediately follows from Theorem 2.6. Using Proposition 7.8 (i) and Lemma 7.10 (i), we see that ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} has neither eigenvalues nor resonance poles near zeros of EB​(λ)E_{\mathrm{B}}(\lambda) except for λ=0,±i​min⁡{1,s}\lambda=0,\pm\mathrm{i}\min\{1,s\}, since 𝒦2​s+k+1​(ν)≠0\mathcal{K}_{2\sqrt{s}+k+1}(\nu)\neq 0 with ν=−k⁡(2​s+k)−1\nu=\sqrt{-k(2\sqrt{s}+k)-1}, k∈{−⌊s⌋,…,−1}k\in\{-\lfloor\sqrt{s}\rfloor,\ldots,-1\}, by (7.30). Using Theorem 2.14 and Lemma 7.10 (iii), we see that ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} also has neither eigenvalues nor resonance poles near zeros of EA​(λ)E_{\mathrm{A}}(\lambda) except for λ=0,±i​min⁡{1,s}\lambda=0,\pm\mathrm{i}\min\{1,s\}. Moreover, the zeros λ=±i​min⁡{1,s}\lambda=\pm\mathrm{i}\min\{1,s\} of E⁡(λ,0)E(\lambda,0) remains purely imaginary by Theorem 2.6. Thus we obtain part (i). For part (ii), using Proposition 7.8 (ii) and Lemma 7.10 (ii), we see that ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} has an eigenvalue with a positive real part near a zero of EB​(λ)E_{\mathrm{B}}(\lambda) with k=ℓk=\ell, since 𝒦2​s+ℓ+1​(ν)≠0\mathcal{K}_{2\sqrt{s}+\ell+1}(\nu)\neq 0 with ν=ℓ⁡(2​s+ℓ)−1\nu=\sqrt{\ell(2\sqrt{s}+\ell)-1} by (7.30). ∎

Remark 7.12.

The nondegenerate condition ℐ(ℓ)≠0\mathcal{I}^{(\ell)}\neq 0 in Proposition 7.8 is not always true. For example, a direct calculation shows

ℐ(2)​(ν4​(λ0),ν2​(λ0))=−4​(s−1)​(s−3)s⁡(s+2)​(s+3)​(2​s−1)​𝒦2​s−1​(4​s−5),\displaystyle\mathcal{I}^{(2)}(\nu_{4}(\lambda_{0}),\nu_{2}(\lambda_{0}))=-\frac{4(\sqrt{s}-1)(\sqrt{s}-3)}{s(\sqrt{s}+2)(\sqrt{s}+3)(2\sqrt{s}-1)}\mathcal{K}_{2\sqrt{s}-1}\Bigl(\sqrt{4\sqrt{s}-5}\Bigr),

where λ0=−i​k​(2​s+k)\lambda_{0}=-\mathrm{i}k(2\sqrt{s}+k) and k=−2k=-2. It vanishes at s=3\sqrt{s}=3. Hence, we could not generally determine whether eigenvalues of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} near λ0=−i​k​(2​s+k)\lambda_{0}=-\mathrm{i}k(2\sqrt{s}+k) with k≠ℓk\neq\ell have positive real parts, in Theorem 7.11 (ii).

Finally, we give some numerical computation results for (ω,s,β2)=(1,4,2)(\omega,s,\beta_{2})=(1,4,2). To obtain these results, we also used the computation tool AUTO [11]. See [38] for the details of our numerical approach and further numerical results. Figure 3 shows how the eigenvalues of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} for the bifurcated solitary wave on each branch change. We only display the eigenvalues with Re​λ,Im​λ≥0\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda,\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda\geq 0 since the spectra of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} are symmetric, as stated in Section 2. For the bifurcated solitary wave born at β1=β1(ℓ)\beta_{1}=\beta_{1}^{(\ell)}, all eigenvalues of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} at β1=β1(ℓ)\beta_{1}=\beta_{1}^{(\ell)} are given by (7.29) and they immediately disappear for k≥ℓk\geq\ell when β1\beta_{1} changes from β1(ℓ)\beta_{1}^{(\ell)} (see Remark 7.9). The loci of the eigenvalues of ℒε\mathscr{L}_{\varepsilon} leaving the imaginary axis from (7.29) when β1\beta_{1} changes from β1(ℓ)\beta_{1}^{(\ell)} are plotted for k=0k=0 and ℓ=1\ell=1 in Fig. 3(a); for k=0,1k=0,1 and ℓ=2\ell=2 in Fig. 3(b); for k=0,1,2k=0,1,2 and ℓ=3\ell=3 in Fig. 3(c); and k=0,1,2,3k=0,1,2,3 and ℓ=4\ell=4 in Figs. 3(d) and (e). Each curve was computed from β1=β1(ℓ)\beta_{1}=\beta_{1}^{(\ell)} to 100100. These results indicate that the real parts of the eigenvalues become positive and the bifurcated solitary waves are unstable when β1≠β1(ℓ)\beta_{1}\neq\beta_{1}^{(\ell)}, as stated in Theorem 7.11.

In Figs. 3(d) and (e) four eigenvalues for the bifurcated solitary wave on the fifth branch (ℓ=4\ell=4) are displayed and their values at β1=β1SN≈19.41626\beta_{1}=\beta_{1}^{\mathrm{SN}}\approx 19.41626, at which a saddle-node bifurcation occurs (see Fig. 2(a)), are plotted as the circle ‘∘\circ’. Especially, the solitary wave seems not to change its stability type at the saddle-node bifurcation point since all the eigenvalues are far from the imaginary axis. On the other hand, the computed eigenvalues at β1=50\beta_{1}=50 and β1=100\beta_{1}=100 were almost the same. So the eigenvalues are thought to converge to certain values as β1→∞\beta_{1}\to\infty. See, e.g., the blue line (k=1k=1) in Fig. 3(b), the blue and green lines (k=1k=1 and 22) in Fig. 3(c), and the green and purple lines (k=2k=2 and 33) in Fig. 3(d).
